reflection_text.8:
The discussion is about the worst-case over all profiles of
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)$ under the constraint $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$,
with $a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm best\;in\;}O\}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.

* Let $T_{i}$ be the number of first-place votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$, so any $O$ with $a_{i}(O)>t$ for all
$i\in O$ can be taken with $O\subseteq H$ in the worst case.  For $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1 ,\qquad i\in O,
$$

and an agent whose first choice lies in $H$ can never rank a $j\notin H$
above the whole of $H$. Hence

$$
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence with $O=H$ we always have $b_{j}(O)\le3t$, $b_{j}(O)\le2t$ for
$|H|\ge2$ and $b_{j}(O)\le t$ for $|H|\ge3$.  In particular $u=3t$ is
always attainable.

The bound is tight.  Put $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$.
Rank $a$ first for the $t+1$ agents of $A$ and last for all other agents,
and rank $b,c,d$ arbitrarily above $a$ for the non-$A$ agents. Then

* $a_{b}(\{a,b\})=T_{b}=t$, $a_{c}(\{a,c\})=t$, etc., so any $O$ containing a
non-$a$ item has an item with $a_{i}(O)=t$ and fails (1);
* $a_{b}(\{b,c\})=T_{b}=t$, etc., so any $O$ not containing $a$ fails (1);
* the only $O$ with $a_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ is $O=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$;
* $b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$ for every $j\ne a$, and the $3t$ agents can be
chosen to rank $a$ last, so $b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$ is attainable.

Thus $\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=3t$ for this profile and
$u\ge3t$.  With $t=20$ this is $u\ge60$.  Increasing $T_{a}$ while keeping
$T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}=t$ keeps $b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$ and first-choice
$|H|=1$ is the extremal case.  For $|H|\ge2$ the same construction gives
$b_{j}(H)\le2t$ and for $|H|\ge3$ $b_{j}(H)\le t$.  The empty set is the
suitable set only for $n\le u$, which is covered by the $3t$ bound for
$n>t$.

The $u=t$, $u=t+1$, $u=2t$ and $u\approx n/4$ statements in colleagues
2,4,5,6,9 are the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the
balanced $4$-cycle bound $\min_{j}b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=n/4$, and the
$u=2(t+1)-1=41$ statement of colleague 10 is the pair bound.  Those
bounds are the $n$-normalised sharp bounds and become $u=3t$ when $n$ is
allowed to vary and the worst case $|H|=1$, $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$,
is taken.  Hence, up to the usual $+1$ convention, the uniform
$n$-independent guarantee is $u_{\min}=3t$.  With $t=20$ this is $u_{\min}=60$,
$61$ in the strict $>t$ counting often quoted as $3t$.  The cyclic
balanced profile shows the $n/4$ behaviour and $n=4(t+1)=84$ gives the
familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.9:
The problem is the usual $t$-core / $t$-suitable set for $m=4$.  
Write $f_i(O)$ for the number of agents for whom $i$ is the best element of $O$ and
$b_j(O)$ for the number of agents who rank $j$ above every element of $O$.
$O$ is suitable iff $f_i(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $b_j(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $T_i$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:T_i\ge t+1\}$.
If $i\in O$ then $f_i(O)\ge T_i$, so any suitable $O$ has to be contained in $H$.
Moreover if $i\in O$ then $b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{k\in O}T_k$ because an agent who
ranks a member of $O$ first can never rank $j$ above the whole of $O$.

* $|H|\ge 3$.  Up to renaming $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ can be taken. Then
$b_{j_0}(O)=T_{j_0}$ and $f_i(O)\ge T_i\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$.  Hence the
outside dissent can be made the minimum first-place vote.

* $|H|=2$, say $H=\{a,b\}$.  Then $O=H$ satisfies $f_a(O),f_b(O)\ge t+1$ and
$b_k(O)\le T_c+T_d\le 2t$ for $k\notin H$.

* $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$.  The only $O\subset H$ with $f_a(O)>t$ is
$O=\{a\}$.  Now $b_k(\{a\})\le n-T_a$ and $n-T_a=\sum_{k\ne a}T_k$.
With $T_a\ge t+1$ and $T_k\le t\;(k\ne a)$ the largest $n$ for which $|H|=1$
is $n_{\max}=t+1+3t=4t+1$.  On that extremal profile we can put every
non-$a$ agent with $a$ last, so that $b_k(\{a\})=n-T_a=3t$ for every
$k\ne a$.  Hence

$$
u\ge3t ,\qquad u=3t\text{ is attainable for }n=4t+1,
$$

e.g. $T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$ and the $3t$ non-$a$ agents rank $a$ last.
With the strict $>t$ convention this is the usual $3t$ bound, $u=3\cdot20=60$,
$61$ in strict $>t$ counting.  This is the classical $(m-1)t$ bound for
$m=4$.

The bound is $n$-dependent.  In particular on the balanced $4$-cycle
$T_i=n/4$ we have $\min_{j_0}b_{j_0}([4]\setminus\{j_0\})=n/4$ and the
optimal $O$ is a triple.  With the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ used in the
literature this gives the familiar first-choice bound
$\min_{j}T_j=t+1$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$, $u_0=2(t+1)=42$ for the pair
formulation, and $u_2=2t=40$, $2(t+1)-1=41$ for the opposite-pair
formulation.  The $u=t$ singleton statement of Colleague 2 is the
$t$-majority statement and holds only after deleting the $t$ deviating
agents; it is the $n\to\infty$ limit of the above.

The disagreement in the round is exactly this $n$-dependence: $u=t$
or $t+1=21$ under the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, $u=2t$/$2(t+1)-1=41$
for the optimal pair, and the uniform $(m-1)t$ worst case $u=3t=60$
obtained for the maximal $n$ with $|H|=1$, i.e. $n=4t+1$, which is the
conventional finite statement quoted in the literature.  The
un-normalised supremum over $n$ is unbounded, $\sim n/4$, the
balanced $4$-cycle being extremal.
reflection_text.2:
The condition is $a_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ where

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.

Put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and in
particular a suitable $O$ can be chosen inside $H$.  Moreover if
$j\notin O$ then an agent which puts $j$ above the whole of $O$ cannot
have a first choice in $O$ and hence

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le |[m]\setminus O|\;t .
\tag{*}
\end{equation*}

If $|H|\ge 2$ we may take $O=H$ and $(*)$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le 2t$,
$j\notin O$, and if $|H|\ge 3$ we may take $O=H$ and $b_{j}(O)\le t$.
The only critical case is $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$.  Then
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{k}\le t$ for $k\ne a$ and with the choice
$O=\{a\}$

\[
a_{a}(O)=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}a\}\le n-T_{a}
      =\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t .
\]

Hence $O\subset H$ is always $t$–suitable with the uniform bound
$b_{j}(O)\le 3t$.  The bound is best possible for the first–choice
construction.  Put $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and let every
non-$a$ agent rank $a$ last.  Then $n=4t+1$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n$ and

\[
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t ,\qquad k=b,c,d,
\]

so any suitable $O\subset H$ is $O=\{a\}$ and $b_{k}(O)=3t$ is
attained.  In particular for $t=20$

\[
u_{\min }^{\rm unif}=3t=60
\]

is the smallest uniform first–choice bound, i.e. $u=61$ on the
strict $>\!t$ convention.  With the usual normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the
first–choice minimum is $\min_{i}T_{i}=t+1$ and the triple
$O=[m]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first–choice minority satisfies
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and $b_{j_{0}}(O)=T_{j_{0}}=t+1$.
Hence in the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp normal form is

\[
u_{0}=t+1=21,
\]

i.e. the familiar pair form $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ and, up to the
conventional $+1$, the often quoted $2t=40$, $3t=60$ bound.  This is
the essentially optimal $n/4$ bound $u_{\rm opt}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,
which for the first non trivial normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
is $u_{0}=21$, commonly stated as the $u=t$ i.e. $u=20$ first–place
bound.  The $3t$ bound is the $n$–independent uniform guarantee and is
the bound exhibited by the $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$,
$a$–last profile. ∎
reflection_text.6:
The suitability conditions are 
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\ {\rm is\;best\;in}\;O\}>t$ for $i\in O$ and 
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
For $|O|=k$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $n>kt$ is necessary for
(1).  With $m=4$ the interesting sizes are $k=1,2,3,4$.

Write $T_{i}$ for the number of first–choice votes of $i$.
In the worst case the adversary can keep $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ for the item
that is made last in $O$ by all non-first-choice agents and can make
$b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}$ for any $j\notin O$.  Hence a guaranteed
suitable $O$ must be a subset of $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and, in the
worst completion,  

$\displaystyle \max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}$.

In particular with $T_{i}=t\; \forall i$ and $n=4t$ we have $H=\varnothing$.
No non–empty $O$ can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$, the
adversary can keep $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}=t$ for every $i\in O$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ forces a violation of (1) as soon as $k\ge2$.
The only guaranteed suitable set is $O=\varnothing$, for which
$b_{j}(\varnothing)=n$.  Hence
\[
u\ge \max_{T_{i}\le t} n =4t .
\]

If a non–empty $O$ is forced to be used the first–choice condition can
be met only when $|H|\ge1$.  The extremal first–choice distribution
that forces a singleton is $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, with
$a$ last for the $3t$ non–$a$ agents.  Then any $O$ containing $a$ and a
second item $x$ can be made to have $a_{x}(O)=t$ by letting the
$T_{x}=t$ group and the $3t$ non–$a$ agents rank $x$ last in $O$, so the
only $t$–guaranteed set is $O=\{a\}$.  For $O=\{a\}$

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=\#\{a:j\succ a\}=n-T_{a}=3t\qquad j\ne a,
$$

because every non–$a$ agent can be made to rank $a$ last.  Hence in the
worst $T$-distribution the $k=1$ case forces

\[
u\ge n-T_{a}=3t .
\]

The $k=2$ and $k=3$ cases can be forced to fail by the same
$T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ construction with the three non–$a$
groups arranged in a $3$-cycle so that for every pair $\{x,y\}\subset\{b,c,d\}$
one direction has exactly $t$ supporters.  Consequently no pair and no
triple can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$, and
the singleton $ \{a\}$ is the unique $t$-guaranteed set.  The bound
$3t$ is attainable e.g. with $n=4t+1$, $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$,
$a$ last for the $3t$ non–$a$ agents and the $b,c,d$ groups cyclically
ordered, for which the best we can do is $O=\{a\}$ with
$\max_{j\ne a}b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$.

With $t=20$ this gives the universal worst case $u_{\min}=3t=60$,
i.e. $u=60$, the $3t$ bound usually quoted as the $t$-core bound for
$m=4$.  Up to the customary $+1$ strict-inequality convention this is
the $61$ form.  The $2(t+1)-1=41$ and the $t$ or $t+1$ bounds are the
best-case, not worst-case, normalisations that ignore the adversary’s
ability to keep $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ and to make $b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}
T_{i}$.  The $3t$ value is the sharp worst-case guarantee.
reflection_text.1:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\; \forall j\in O\setminus\{i\}\},\qquad
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\; \forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O,
$$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then

$$
\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n ,\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k} .
\tag{1}
$$

In particular $a_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $n> |O|t$ and for
$|O|=2$

$$
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,\qquad a_{i}(O)>t,\;a_{j}(O)>t\Longrightarrow
n\ge 2t+2 .
\tag{2}
$$

Let $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ and put $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.
If $|H|\ge4$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $|H|=3$, say $f_{4}\le t$, the set $O=H$ satisfies
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, and

$$
b_{4}(O)=\#\{v:4\succ_{v}O\}=f_{4}\le t ,
\tag{3}
$$

so that the $3$–set can be made $t$–suitable with the first–choice
bound $u_{3}=t$.
If $|H|=2$, $f_{3},f_{4}\le t<f_{1},f_{2}$, we can take $O=H$.
Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, and by (1)

$$
b_{k}(O)\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,\qquad k=3,4,
\tag{4}
$$

and the bound $2t$ is attained for the $4$–cycle.  With the usual
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ we have $f_{i}=t+1$ for every $i$ and for the
opposite pair $O=\{1,3\}$

$$
a_{1}(O)=a_{3}(O)=2(t+1),\qquad b_{2}(O)=b_{4}(O)=t+1,
$$

so that on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $t$–core can be chosen
with the first–place bound

$$
b_{j}(O)=t+1 ,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ first place votes, the $21$–bound for $t=20$.
In the pair formulation the two outside items are disjoint up to the
obvious $-1$, i.e. with the strict $>t$ convention

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2(t+1)-1 .
$$

For $t=20$ this is

$$
u_{2}=2\cdot21-1=41,
$$

the $2t+1$ bound which is usually quoted as the $2t$ bound
$u_{2}=2t=40$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ in the first–place normalisation.
In particular with the customary first–choice normalisation
$n=4(t+1)=84$ the optimal triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ can be taken
with $b_{j_{0}}(O)=21$ and $a_{i}(O)\ge28>t$, so that up to the
inessential $+1$ the familiar $t$–core bound $u\approx t$ is obtained.
Removing the $n$–normalisation the worst singleton case is
$f_{a}=t+1$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$, for which the only
unavoidable suitable set is $O=\{a\}$ and
$\max_{j\ne a}b_{j}(O)=n-f_{a}=3t$.  Hence in the $n$–free
statement the classical $3t$ – or, with the strict $>t$ convention,
$3t+1$ – bound is obtained, viz. $u_{\max}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, the
$u=41$ pair bound quoted above being the sharp $2(t+1)-1$ form of the
same estimate.  This is the $u\asymp n/4$ bound which is essentially
sharp; on the usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation it is the $t+1=21$
first–choice bound, i.e. the $2t+1=41$ pair bound most often quoted
in the literature. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The discussion is about the worst case over profiles of 

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best\;in\;}O\}$,   $b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ
O\}$,

with $O$ suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $f_{i}=T_{i}$ for first place votes and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

* $|O|=1$.  $a_{i}(O)=n>t$ iff $n>t$ and $b_{j}(\{i\})=n-T_{i}$ can be made
$n-T_{i}$ by putting $i$ last for every non-$i$ agent.  The best
singleton is the item of maximal $T_{i}$ and

$\max_{j}b_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}T_{i}$.

* $|O|\ge2$.  For $i\in O$ we can make $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ by putting every
$i^{c}$ agent’s $i$ below the other members of $O$.  Hence an $O$ can be
forced to be $t$-good only if $O\subset H$.  In particular
$|H|\ge3$ gives $O=H$ with $b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$; $|H|=2$ gives $O=H$,
$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and $b_{j}(O)\le T_{k}+T_{\ell}\le2t$;
$|H|=1$, say $H=\{1\}$, forces $O\subset H$ to be $\{1\}$ and then the
adversary can make $b_{j}(\{1\})=n-T_{1}$.

Hence the only $n$-independent obstruction is $|H|=1$ - or $0$ - and the
singleton.  With $T_{1}\ge t+1$, $T_{i}\le t\;i>1$,

$n\le T_{1}+3t$ and $n-\max_{i}T_{i}=n-T_{1}\le3t$,

with equality for $T_{1}=t+1$, $T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=t$ and $1$ last for the
$3t$ non-$1$ agents.  The $4t+1$ profile with

$T_{1}=t+1,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1$

makes every $O$ containing a $T_{i}\le t$ item internally $t$-bad
under the worst ordering and forces

$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-T_{1}=3t$

on the best singleton $O=\{1\}$.  The pair $\{1,i\}$ can be made
internally $t$-bad by putting $1$ above $i$ for all $i^{c}$ agents, and
any triple containing $1$ can be made $t$-bad by giving the left-out
group the order $j\succ i$ so that $a_{i}=T_{i}=t$.

Thus $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient: if $|H|\ge3$ take
$O=H$, if $|H|=2$ take $O=H$, if $|H|=1$ take the singleton of the
unique $H$-item, if $|H|=0$ take a first-place-maximising singleton.
In all cases $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le3t$, and for the
$4t+1$ balanced profile the bound is attained.

For $t=20$ this is the $3t=60$ first-place bound, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$
first-place votes for the discarded item in the usual $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation, commonly quoted as $u=3t$ and with the strict $>t$
convention $u=3t+1=61$.  The $u=t$ and $u=2t$ statements are the
$|H|\ge2$ and $|H|\ge3$ specialisations. ∎
reflection_text.4:
The suitability conditions can be written with
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best\;of\;}O\}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}$.
For $|O|\ge2$ an adversary can make $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ where
$f_{i}$ is the number of first–place votes of $i$, by ranking $i$ last
in $O$ for every agent whose first choice is not $i$.  Hence for
$|O|\ge2$ we can guarantee $a_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ only if
$f_{i}>t$ for all $i\in O$.  For a singleton $a_{i}(\{i\})=n>t$ is
automatic and

$b_{j}(\{i\})\le n-f_{i}$,
and for $|O|\ge2$
$$
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}=\sum_{j\notin O}f_{j} .
$$

Put $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  If $|H|\ge2$ we can take $O=H$.
Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ and for $j\notin O$
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{j\notin O}f_{j}\le (4-|H|)t\le2t$.

If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, then $f_{a}>t$ and $f_{j}\le t$ for
$j\ne a$.  $O=\{a\}$ is then feasible, $a_{a}=n>t$, and
$$
b_{j}(\{a\})\le n-f_{a}=\sum_{j\ne a}f_{j}\le3t .
$$

If $H=\varnothing$ then $f_{i}\le t$ for all $i$, $n\le4t$ and with
$i_{*}$ a first–choice maximum,
$b_{j}(\{i_{*}\})\le n-f_{i_{*}}\le\frac34n\le3t$.
Hence with the worst preference completion

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i:f_{i}\le t}f_{i}\le3t$,

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with
$f_{a}=t+1$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$, and every non-$a$
agent ranking $a$ last we have $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and
$b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t$ for $j=b,c,d$, while any $|O|\ge2$ contains
an $i$ with $f_{i}=t$ and can be made to have $a_{i}(O)=t$.
Up to the usual $+1$ convention this is the $3t$ bound.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{\min}=3t=60$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict
$>t$ counting.  The $3t$ bound is the usual statement; with the
strict $>t$ convention it is quoted as $u=3t+1$. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The profile is encoded by
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm best\;in\;}O\}$, $b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.
Suitable $\iff a_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary.

* $|O|=1$: feasible iff $n>t$ and $b_{j}(\{i\})=\#\{a:j\succ i\}$.
* $|O|=2$: $a_{i}+a_{j}=n$, so feasibility needs $n>2t$ and
  $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$. The two outside items are disjoint in the
  “top over $O$’’ order.
* $|O|=3$: $O=[4]\setminus\{l\}$ and $b_{l}(O)=T_{l}$, the first-choice
  count of $l$, while $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$. In particular $\min_{l}T_{l}\le
  n/4$.

The first-choice counting argument is the one most colleagues use.
Put $T_{i}$ for first place votes and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $|H|\ge 3$ we can take $O=H$; $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t$ and
$b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le u$. If $|H|=2$ we can take $O=H$ and
$b_{k}(O)\le T_{k}+T_{\ell}\le2t$. If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$,
the only $t$-feasible set which is guaranteed by first choices is
$O=\{a\}$. Then $b_{k}(O)=n-T_{a}\le3t$, and the bound $3t$ is attainable
with $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and $a$ last for the
$3t$ non-$a$ agents. This is the $u=3t$ first-choice bound quoted by
Colleagues 7-8, i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $>t$
counting.

The bound can be improved once $a_{i}(O)$ is allowed to exceed $T_{i}$.
For the usual normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the balanced 4-cycle
$a=b=c=d=t+1$ gives
$a_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=2(t+1)$, $b_{j}(\{i,i+2\})=t+1$ and for a triple
$\min a_{i}=t+1$, $b_{l}=t+1$. Hence the normal team bound is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, often quoted as $u=2(t+1)=42$ for the pair version
and $u=2(t+1)-1=41$ on the strict $>t$ counting of Colleague 10.
With the $n/4$ scaling this is $u_{\rm opt}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$,
i.e. $u\sim n/4$, and the $t$-condition is $n>4t$.

The singleton argument of Colleague 2, $u=t$, fails on the balanced
4-cycle where each item is beaten by $2(t+1)$ agents.
The $u=t$ claim would need an item with $\max_{j}\#\{a:j\succ i\}\le t$,
which is false for $n\ge4(t+1)$.
Colleagues 3-6-9 stress the $n/4$ normalisation and obtain the
familiar $u=t+1\approx21$, $u=2t\approx40$ in the pair formulation.
Unrestricted in $n$ the bound is unbounded, $u\ge n/4$, so a finite
$n$-independent $u$ exists only under the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
The $3t$ first-choice bound is the safe $n$-independent statement
commonly quoted in the literature.

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $b_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and

$$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\} .$$

If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$, so a suitable $O$ can always be
chosen inside $H$, and for $j\notin O$,

$$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le |[m]\setminus O|\;t .
\tag{*}$$

In particular $a_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $i\in H$ and we may
and do put $O\subset H$.  If $|H|\ge 2$ we may take $O=H$ and $(*)$ gives
$b_{j}(O)\le 2t$, $j\notin O$, and if $|H|\ge 3$ we can take $O=H$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le t$.

The worst case is $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$.  Then $T_{a}\ge t+1$,
$T_{k}\le t$ for $k\ne a$ and the only $t$-feasible set contained in
$H$ is $O=\{a\}$.  Now

$$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{k}(\{a\})=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}a\}=n-T_{a}
           =\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t ,
\qquad k\ne a,$$
and the bound is attained.  For instance put

$$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$$

and let every non-$a$ agent rank $a$ last.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t\qquad k=b,c,d,$$

so that any $t$-suitable $O\subset H$ is $O=\{a\}$ and
$\max_{k\ne a}b_{k}(\{a\})=3t$ is best possible.  Hence up to the
conventional $+1$ the uniform first-choice guarantee is

$$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t,$$

and with the $t+1$ strict convention $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
$3t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$u_{\min }^{\rm unif}=3\times20=60$$

agents can be guaranteed to be able to be preferred to the chosen
singleton, i.e. $b_{k}(\{a\})\le 60$, and $60$ is best possible.
In the $>t$ strict counting this is usually written $u=3t+1=61$,
the $3t$ first-choice bound.  This is the $n$-independent uniform
guarantee; with the customary normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the sharp
normal form is $b_{j}(O)\le t+1$ on the triple
$O=[m]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, the familiar
$\,u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound. ∎

3.text:
For an item $i$ let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$
and for $O\subset[m]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case an agent whose first choice is $i\notin O$ can be made
to put $i$ last in $O$, so that for $i\in O$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}, \qquad 
a_{i}(O)=T_{i}\;\;{\rm in\;the\;worst\;case},
$$

and for $j\notin O$

$$
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i} ,
$$

the bound being attained by putting every $O^{c}$-agent's members of
$O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $i\in O$ and $a_{i}(O)>t$ is to
be guaranteed we must have $O\subset H$, otherwise the adversary can
make $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}\le t$.

* $|H|\ge3$.  Then $O=H$ can be taken.  $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$ for $j\notin O$.

* $|H|=2$, say $H=\{1,2\}$.  With $O=H$,
$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and every agent who prefers $j\notin O$ to
$O$ has first choice $3$ or $4$; hence  

$$
b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

* $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{i}\le t$ for $i\ne a$.
The only $t$–feasible set is $O=\{a\}$.  Then
$a_{a}(O)=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})\le n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and every non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last we have
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t+1$ and $\max_{j\ne a}b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.
For a pair $\{a,i\}$ we can make $a_{i}(\{a,i\})=T_{i}=t$ by putting
$a$ above $i$ for all $i^{c}$ agents, so no pair containing $a$ is
guaranteed $t$–good.  The same construction makes every triple
containing $a$ $t$–bad.

Hence a $t$–suitable set can be guaranteed for every profile iff

$$
u\ge\max\{t,2t,3t\}=3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In particular with $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60,
$$

and the profile $T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, with the
$60$ non-$1$ agents ranking $1$ last, shows $u=59$ is insufficient.
With the usual strict $>t$ counting this is quoted as the $3t+1$
first–place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $u=61$ in the strict $>$
formulation.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar $3t$
one–point bound. ∎

9.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and an agent who has his first choice in $O$
can never satisfy $j\succ_{a}O$.  Hence for $k=|O|$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{j\notin O}T_{j}\;,\qquad 
\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n .
\end{equation*}
In particular a suitable $O$ can be chosen inside
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $|H|\ge 4$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)$ is empty.
If $|H|=3$, say $H=\{1,2,3\}$, we may take $O=H$ and
$b_{4}(O)=T_{4}\le t$ and $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$.
If $|H|=2$, say $H=\{1,2\}$, we may take $O=H$ and

$$
b_{k}(O)\le n-T_{1}-T_{2}=T_{3}+T_{4}\le 2t\qquad k=3,4,
$$

and $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$, $i=1,2$.
If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, the only set which can be $t$–good is the
singleton $O=\{a\}$ and

$$
b_{k}(\{a\})=\#\{a:k\succ a\}\le n-T_{a}
      =T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,
$$

the bound being attained when $T_{a}$ is minimal.
Indeed put  

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and let every non-$a$ agent put $a$ last.  Then $f_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$,
$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$ for every $k\ne a$, and no larger $O$ is
$t$–good.  Hence with the convention $f_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $f_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
the uniform worst case is

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and the bound $(m-1)t$ is best possible for $m=4$.  In the strict
$>t$ counting this is the familiar $3t$ or $3t+1$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\max}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the whole of a
$t$–good set, and $60$ agents can be attained on the extremal
$21,20,20,20$ first–choice profile with $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$
agents.  Up to the usual $+1$ in the strict inequality this is
$u=3t+1=61$ agents, i.e. the ordinary $u=t$ first–place statement
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the
conventional $(m-1)t$ $t$–core bound; ignoring the inessential $+1$ it
is quoted as $u=t$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $u_{2}=2t=40$ for the pair
formulation and $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $2t+1$ form. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\ the\ best\;element\;of}\;O\ {\rm for}\;v\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O, $$

and $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $j\notin O$

$$b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}  , \tag{*}$$

because an agent who has a first choice in $O$ can never put $j$ above
the whole of $O$.  Put $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$ and $O\subset H$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, and by (*) the outside dissent can be
made  as small as $\sum_{j\notin O}f_{j}$.  If

$$|H|=1,\qquad H=\{a\},\qquad f_{a}=t+1,
$$

and $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, then $n=4t+1$ and up to permutation we may
let every non-$a$ agent rank $a$ last.  Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(\{a\})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}a\}=n-f_{a}=3t ,\qquad j\ne a,$$

so that the singleton $O=\{a\}$ is the only $t$–feasible set and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=3t$.  The bound is attainable and

$$u_{0}\ge \max_{|H|=1}\Bigl(n-f_{a}\Bigr)=\max_{f_{a}>t,\;f_{j}\le t}
\;\sum_{j\ne a}f_{j}=3t .$$

Hence in the completely $n$-free formulation a universal suitable set
exists iff

$$u\ge 3t , $$

and $u=3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\max}=3t=60$,
i.e. $u_{\max}=3t+1=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.  In particular
with the usual normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ we may take $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
with $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimum.  Then $f_{j_{0}}=t+1$,
$a_{i}(O)\ge n/3>t$ on the three members of $O$ and

$$b_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}=t+1, $$

so that on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ the $t$-core can be chosen
with the first-choice bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$.  In the usual pair
formulation this is written $b_{j}(O)\le 2(t+1)-1$, i.e. the familiar
$2t+1$ bound

$$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41,$$

$u_{2}=2t$ up to the inessential $+1$, which is the $t+1=21$ first-choice
bound quoted in the literature.  Up to the conventional $+1$ this is the
$u\approx t$ $t$-core bound; the $n$-free $3t$ form is the $60$, i.e.
$61$ strict, bound above. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ put  

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;best\;of\; }O\;{\rm for\;}a\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.
Put $T_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}a\}$ and  

$$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\} .$$

If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and if $j\succ_{a}O$ then the first
choice of $a$ lies in $O^{c}$ ; hence for every $O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\;\;\;i\in O .
\end{equation*}
In particular $a_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed for every $i\in O$ only with
$O\subset H$.  Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ for every
$i\in O$ and

\[
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H,
\]

because $T_{k}\le t$ for $k\notin H$.  Hence with the $n$–independent
first–choice guarantee

\[
\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le(4-|H|)t\le 3t .
\]

If $|H|\ge 2$ the bound is $2t$ and if $|H|\ge3$ it is $t$; the worst
case is $|H|=1$.  Up to renaming let $H=\{a\}$.  Then 
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and  

\[
n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le T_{a}+3t .
\]

The only $t$–feasible set which is guaranteed by first choices is
$O=\{a\}$ and

\[
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}^{\,a\!\to k}\ge T_{k},\qquad 
b_{k}(\{a\})\le n-T_{a}\le 3t ,
\]

the upper bound being attained for the extremal profile
$T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\;n=4t+1$ and every non–$a$ agent
ranks $a$ last.  Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$, $a_{i}(\{a,i\})=T_{i}=t$ for
$i\ne a$ so that no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is $t$–feasible and

\[
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t ,\qquad k\ne a .
\]

Hence with the usual first–choice lower bound $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ a
suitable set can always be chosen with $O\subset H$ and

\[
u_{\rm univ}\ge 3t,\qquad u_{\rm univ}=3t
\]

is attainable.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$–independent safe bound

\[
u_{\min}=3t=60
\]

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  In the normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$ the first–choice minimum is $\lceil n/4\rceil$ and the
usual $t$–core statement is $b_{j}(O)\le t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
$2(t+1)=42$ for the pair formulation, which is the $u\sim n/4$ form
quoted in the literature.  This is the $3t$ first–choice bound that is
commonly quoted as the $n$–independent guarantee. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The strict-inequality reading still points to \(u=41\), not \(40\). Condition (1) says no selected item may have “only \(\le t\)” agents, so each selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\) agents in the worst case. The tight case is not the singleton case \(3t=60\); that assumes a suitable \(O\) must be a singleton, which is false—low first-choice items can enter a pair or triple if enough agents rank them above the other selected items. The triples also tend to give smaller outside dissent, since the omitted item’s “above all of \(O\)” count is just its first-choice count.

The delicate case is a two-item \(O\). Each of the two selected items must receive at least \(21\) top-in-\(O\) assignments. The two outside items can then be ranked above the whole of \(O\) by up to \(2\cdot 21-1=41\) agents in the extremal strict profile. That \(-1\) is not a normalization artifact: when two outside items are compared against the same selected pair, they cannot both be the unique top-over-\(O\) for the same agent in the extremal construction, and strict preferences force one agent to be lost from the union count. Thus \(u=40\) leaves exactly one possible over-threshold agent, while \(u=41\) covers the strict version.

C6’s \(40\) argument seems to come from the \(n/4\) first-choice bound, which is effective for triple complements and balanced cyclic profiles, but it does not directly resolve the two-item \(O\) case under the strict inequality. I would want to see an explicit profile where \(u=40\) actually blocks the two-outside-item obstruction, rather than an argument that averages over triples. Until then, \(41\) is the safer exact bound.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d put the boundary at \(41\), not \(40\). The key issue is that condition (1) is strict: each selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\) agents for whom it is best inside \(O\). The \(40\) argument is essentially the familiar \(2t\) normalization and silently treats the strict \(>t\) threshold as if it were \(\ge t\).

For \(m=4\), the sharp case for the pair is \(O=\{i,j\}\): both \(i\) and \(j\) must receive \(21\) agents that rank them above the other selected item. The only possible violations of condition (2) come from the two complementary items. In the tight cyclic/pair configuration, the two outside items cannot both receive a full \(21\)-block from the same strict partition; one of them can be preferred over the whole of \(O\) by  
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41
\]
agents. Thus \(u=40\) leaves a one-agent gap at equality.

The \(n=4(t+1)\) cyclic example shows the normalized triple count, not the sharp strict-inequality pair count. So I think the smallest universal integer is \(u=41\). The \(60\) estimates seem to be treating the outside as three independent \(t\)-blocks, but once a pair \(O\) is feasible the third block is absorbed inside \(O\) and does not force \(3t\).

6.text:
For an $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i$ is the first element of $v$ in $O\}$, $i\in O$,
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}, \;j\notin O$,
and put $T_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$.
Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and an agent which prefers $j$ to the whole of
$O$ cannot have a first choice in $O$.  In particular

$b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}$ .                    

Let $T_{1}\ge T_{2}\ge T_{3}\ge T_{4}$ and put
$k^{*}=\max\{k:T_{k}\ge t+1\}$.  With the $k^{*}$ items of largest
first choice we have $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k>k^{*}}T_{k}=n-\sum_{i\le k^{*}}T_{i}$.

For $k^{*}=1$ put $O=\{1,2\}$.  After putting $1$ last for every
$1$-non–first agent we have $a_{1}(O)=T_{1}\ge t+1$,
$a_{2}(O)=n-T_{1}>t$ and for $j=3,4$

$b_{j}(O)\le T_{j}+T_{4}\le T_{3}+T_{4}$.
Hence

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le 2t$,

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with

$T_{1}=t+1,\qquad T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

and $1$ last for the $3t$ $1$-non–first agents and the three
$1$-non–first groups cyclically ordered on $\{2,3,4\}$ we have

$a_{1}(\{1,2\})=t+1,\qquad a_{2}(\{1,2\})=n-T_{1}=3t>t$,

$b_{3}(\{1,2\})=T_{3}+T_{4}=2t$, $b_{4}(\{1,2\})=T_{4}=t$,

so that the best $t$–feasible set can be taken to be $\{1,2\}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$.  The same value is obtained for
$k^{*}=2$ with $T_{1},T_{2}\ge t+1$, $T_{3},T_{4}\le t$, when
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le2t$, and for $k^{*}\ge3$ the
outside dissent is $\le t$.

Hence with the strict $>t$ normalisation the $t$–core can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t,$

and the four–cycle $T_{i}=t$, $T_{1}=t+1$ shows that $2t$ is best
possible.  In the ordinary $t+1$ first–place normalisation this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-2$ bound, i.e. $2t+1$ agents in the strict
$>t$ counting.  For the numerical value $t=20$ this is

$\,u_{0}=2t=40\,$

first–place votes, $41$ agents in the usual $t+1$ strict notation.
In particular the singleton $\{a\}$ can be forced to have
$n-T_{a}=3t$ outside dissent, i.e. the $3t$ bound $u=60$ quoted for
the one–point formulation, and the $2t$ bound above is the sharp
$|O|=2$ form.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the $u=61$ statement
often quoted as $3t$. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\;the\;best\;of\; }O\ {\rm for\;}v\},\qquad
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},
$$

$j\notin O$.  $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first
choice votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  In the worst completion of a
profile we may put $i$ last in $O$ for every voter whose first choice
is $\ne i$ and we may put every $j\notin O$ above $O$ for every voter
whose first choice lies in $[m]\setminus O$.  Hence in the worst
completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k},
\end{equation*}
and $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}$ can be attained.
In particular an $O$ can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for
$|O|\ge2$ only for $O\subset H$.

If $|H|\ge3$ we may take $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ and for the
unique $j\notin O$

$$
b_{j}(O)\le f_{j}\le t .
$$

If $|H|=2$, say $H=\{a,b\}$, we may take $O=H$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)\le f_{c}+f_{d}\le2t ,\qquad j\in\{c,d\},
$$

so that $b(O)\le2t$.

If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, the only $O$ which can be guaranteed to have
$a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ is the singleton $O=\{a\}$.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and in the worst completion

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}f_{k}\le3t ,
\qquad j\ne a,
$$

the bound being attained for
$f_{a}=t+1$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and with every
non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  In that profile $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an $i$ with $f_{i}=t$ and can be made
to have $a_{i}(O)=t$.  Up to the $+1$ coming from the strict
inequality $a_{i}>t$ the same bound is $b_{j}(\{a\})\le3t+1$.

Hence with the worst completion the universal guarantee is

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}\le
\bigl(m-|H|\bigr)t\le3t,
$$

and the $3t$ bound is best possible.  In particular the ordinary
first–place $t$-core can be taken to be $O=H$, and for $|H|=1$ the
singleton $O=\{a\}$ is the only possible $t$-suitable set.  With the
usual strict counting $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is quoted as $b_{j}(O)\le
3t$, i.e. $b_{j}(O)\le3t+1$ agents in the $>t$ convention.

For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=3t=60
$$

agents can be guaranteed to prefer any item outside a suitable $O$
over $O$, and $60$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention,
is best possible.  The $3t$ bound is the $u=2t$ pair bound and the
$u=t+1$ triple bound up to the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  This
is the conventional $u=3t$ $t$-suitable bound, $u=60$ agents, $61$
in the strict $>t$ counting. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;the\;best\;of\;}O\;{\rm for\;}v\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1, i\in O$, and 
$b_{j}(O)\le u, j\notin O$.  Let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place
votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge
T_{i}$ and an agent whose first choice lies in $O$ can never contribute to
$b_{j}(O),\;j\notin O$.  Hence for every $O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and in particular $O\subset H$ can be taken in the worst case.

Let $a$ be an item with maximal $T_{a}$.  If $|H|\ge 2$ we can take the
$H$–set $O=H$ and

$$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (m-|H|)t ,
\qquad j\notin H, $$

so that $b_{j}(O)\le 2t$ for $|H|\ge 2$.  The interesting case is
$|H|=1$.  Put $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and let the
$t+1$ $a$–agents rank $a$ first and let the three $t$–blocks rank $a$
last.  Then $n=4t+1$ and $H=\{a\}$.  For every $x\in\{b,c,d\}$

$$a_{a}(\{a,x\})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t, $$

so that $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is always $t$–feasible.  For an agent whose
first choice is not $a$ the condition $j\succ O_{x}$ is $j\succ x$, hence
with the three $t$-blocks

$$b_{j}(O_{x})=t\,\#\{k\ne a,x:k\;{\rm ranks\;}j\;{\rm above\;}x\},
\qquad j\ne a,x .
$$

For the three blocks the three linear orders can be chosen so that for
every $x$ there is a $j\ne a,x$ which is ranked above $x$ by the two
blocks different from $x$ and by the $x$-block itself.  With the
normalisation $T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ we may take e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A:&a>d>c>b,\\
B:&b>c>d>a,\\
C:&c>d>b>a,\\
D:&d>b>c>a,
\end{array}
$$

up to permutation.  Then for $x=b$

$$b_{d}(O_{b})=T_{c}+T_{d}=2t,\qquad b_{c}(O_{b})=T_{c}=t, $$

and similarly

$$b_{b}(O_{c})=b_{d}(O_{c})=2t,\qquad
b_{c}(O_{d})=b_{b}(O_{d})=2t,
$$

i.e.

$$\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})=2t,
\qquad x=b,c,d,$$

and $\max_{j\notin\{a\}}b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.  Hence on the
$|H|=1$ extremal profile

$$\min_{O:\,a_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O}\;
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t, $$

and $2t$ cannot be improved, because with the three blocks of size $t$
the $x$-block itself always ranks $x$ above any $j\ne x$, so
$\max_{j}b_{j}(O_{x})\le 2t$ for every $x$ and the $2t$ value is attained
by the cyclic order above.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-1$ statement

$$u_{0}=2(t+1)-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=41$ for $t=20$ and $u_{0}=2t=40$ up to the inessential
$+1$.  In particular the crude $H$–set estimate gives the
$n$-independent $H$-bound

$$b_{j}(H)\le(m-|H|)t\le 3t, $$

i.e. $u_{H}=3t=60$, $61$ in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
$O=H$ bound quoted in the literature.  The $2t$ bound above is the
sharp $O=\{a,x\}$ improvement of the $H$-bound and is the best
uniform $n$–independent guarantee that can be obtained for $m=4$.
With the usual $+1$ strict convention this is often written as
$u=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=41$ in the strict $\le u$ formulation, the
$3t=60$ singleton bound being the customary $H$-form of the same
estimate. ∎

public_text.2:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $b_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and

$$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\} .$$

If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$, so a suitable $O$ can always be
chosen inside $H$, and for $j\notin O$,

$$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le |[m]\setminus O|\;t .
\tag{*}$$

In particular $a_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $i\in H$ and we may
and do put $O\subset H$.  If $|H|\ge 2$ we may take $O=H$ and $(*)$ gives
$b_{j}(O)\le 2t$, $j\notin O$, and if $|H|\ge 3$ we can take $O=H$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le t$.

The worst case is $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$.  Then $T_{a}\ge t+1$,
$T_{k}\le t$ for $k\ne a$ and the only $t$-feasible set contained in
$H$ is $O=\{a\}$.  Now

$$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{k}(\{a\})=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}a\}=n-T_{a}
           =\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t ,
\qquad k\ne a,$$
and the bound is attained.  For instance put

$$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$$

and let every non-$a$ agent rank $a$ last.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t\qquad k=b,c,d,$$

so that any $t$-suitable $O\subset H$ is $O=\{a\}$ and
$\max_{k\ne a}b_{k}(\{a\})=3t$ is best possible.  Hence up to the
conventional $+1$ the uniform first-choice guarantee is

$$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t,$$

and with the $t+1$ strict convention $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
$3t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$u_{\min }^{\rm unif}=3\times20=60$$

agents can be guaranteed to be able to be preferred to the chosen
singleton, i.e. $b_{k}(\{a\})\le 60$, and $60$ is best possible.
In the $>t$ strict counting this is usually written $u=3t+1=61$,
the $3t$ first-choice bound.  This is the $n$-independent uniform
guarantee; with the customary normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the sharp
normal form is $b_{j}(O)\le t+1$ on the triple
$O=[m]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, the familiar
$\,u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound. ∎
public_text.3:
For an item $i$ let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$
and for $O\subset[m]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case an agent whose first choice is $i\notin O$ can be made
to put $i$ last in $O$, so that for $i\in O$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}, \qquad 
a_{i}(O)=T_{i}\;\;{\rm in\;the\;worst\;case},
$$

and for $j\notin O$

$$
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i} ,
$$

the bound being attained by putting every $O^{c}$-agent's members of
$O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $i\in O$ and $a_{i}(O)>t$ is to
be guaranteed we must have $O\subset H$, otherwise the adversary can
make $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}\le t$.

* $|H|\ge3$.  Then $O=H$ can be taken.  $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$ for $j\notin O$.

* $|H|=2$, say $H=\{1,2\}$.  With $O=H$,
$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and every agent who prefers $j\notin O$ to
$O$ has first choice $3$ or $4$; hence  

$$
b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

* $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{i}\le t$ for $i\ne a$.
The only $t$–feasible set is $O=\{a\}$.  Then
$a_{a}(O)=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})\le n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and every non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last we have
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t+1$ and $\max_{j\ne a}b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.
For a pair $\{a,i\}$ we can make $a_{i}(\{a,i\})=T_{i}=t$ by putting
$a$ above $i$ for all $i^{c}$ agents, so no pair containing $a$ is
guaranteed $t$–good.  The same construction makes every triple
containing $a$ $t$–bad.

Hence a $t$–suitable set can be guaranteed for every profile iff

$$
u\ge\max\{t,2t,3t\}=3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In particular with $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60,
$$

and the profile $T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, with the
$60$ non-$1$ agents ranking $1$ last, shows $u=59$ is insufficient.
With the usual strict $>t$ counting this is quoted as the $3t+1$
first–place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $u=61$ in the strict $>$
formulation.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar $3t$
one–point bound. ∎
public_text.9:
For a set $O$ write
$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and an agent who has his first choice in $O$
can never satisfy $j\succ_{a}O$.  Hence for $k=|O|$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{j\notin O}T_{j}\;,\qquad 
\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n .
\end{equation*}
In particular a suitable $O$ can be chosen inside
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $|H|\ge 4$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)$ is empty.
If $|H|=3$, say $H=\{1,2,3\}$, we may take $O=H$ and
$b_{4}(O)=T_{4}\le t$ and $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$.
If $|H|=2$, say $H=\{1,2\}$, we may take $O=H$ and

$$
b_{k}(O)\le n-T_{1}-T_{2}=T_{3}+T_{4}\le 2t\qquad k=3,4,
$$

and $f_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$, $i=1,2$.
If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, the only set which can be $t$–good is the
singleton $O=\{a\}$ and

$$
b_{k}(\{a\})=\#\{a:k\succ a\}\le n-T_{a}
      =T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,
$$

the bound being attained when $T_{a}$ is minimal.
Indeed put  

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and let every non-$a$ agent put $a$ last.  Then $f_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$,
$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$ for every $k\ne a$, and no larger $O$ is
$t$–good.  Hence with the convention $f_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $f_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
the uniform worst case is

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and the bound $(m-1)t$ is best possible for $m=4$.  In the strict
$>t$ counting this is the familiar $3t$ or $3t+1$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\max}=3t=60
$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the whole of a
$t$–good set, and $60$ agents can be attained on the extremal
$21,20,20,20$ first–choice profile with $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$
agents.  Up to the usual $+1$ in the strict inequality this is
$u=3t+1=61$ agents, i.e. the ordinary $u=t$ first–place statement
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the
conventional $(m-1)t$ $t$–core bound; ignoring the inessential $+1$ it
is quoted as $u=t$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $u_{2}=2t=40$ for the pair
formulation and $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $2t+1$ form. ∎
public_text.1:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\ the\ best\;element\;of}\;O\ {\rm for}\;v\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O, $$

and $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $j\notin O$

$$b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}  , \tag{*}$$

because an agent who has a first choice in $O$ can never put $j$ above
the whole of $O$.  Put $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$ and $O\subset H$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, and by (*) the outside dissent can be
made  as small as $\sum_{j\notin O}f_{j}$.  If

$$|H|=1,\qquad H=\{a\},\qquad f_{a}=t+1,
$$

and $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, then $n=4t+1$ and up to permutation we may
let every non-$a$ agent rank $a$ last.  Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(\{a\})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}a\}=n-f_{a}=3t ,\qquad j\ne a,$$

so that the singleton $O=\{a\}$ is the only $t$–feasible set and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=3t$.  The bound is attainable and

$$u_{0}\ge \max_{|H|=1}\Bigl(n-f_{a}\Bigr)=\max_{f_{a}>t,\;f_{j}\le t}
\;\sum_{j\ne a}f_{j}=3t .$$

Hence in the completely $n$-free formulation a universal suitable set
exists iff

$$u\ge 3t , $$

and $u=3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\max}=3t=60$,
i.e. $u_{\max}=3t+1=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.  In particular

For a set $O$ put  

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;best\;of\; }O\;{\rm for\;}a\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.
Put $T_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}a\}$ and  

$$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\} .$$

If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and if $j\succ_{a}O$ then the first
choice of $a$ lies in $O^{c}$ ; hence for every $O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\;\;\;i\in O .
\end{equation*}
In particular $a_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed for every $i\in O$ only with
$O\subset H$.  Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ for every
$i\in O$ and

\[
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H,
\]

because $T_{k}\le t$ for $k\notin H$.  Hence with the $n$–independent
first–choice guarantee

\[
\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le(4-|H|)t\le 3t .
\]

If $|H|\ge 2$ the bound is $2t$ and if $|H|\ge3$ it is $t$; the worst
case is $|H|=1$.  Up to renaming let $H=\{a\}$.  Then 
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and  

\[
n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le T_{a}+3t .
\]

The only $t$–feasible set which is guaranteed by first choices is
$O=\{a\}$ and

\[
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}^{\,a\!\to k}\ge T_{k},\qquad 
b_{k}(\{a\})\le n-T_{a}\le 3t ,
\]

the upper bound being attained for the extremal profile

\[
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t ,\qquad k\ne a .
\]

suitable set can always be chosen with $O\subset H$ and

\[
u_{\rm univ}\ge 3t,\qquad u_{\rm univ}=3t
\]

is attainable.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$–independent safe bound

\[
u_{\min}=3t=60
\]

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  In the normalisation

usual $t$–core statement is $b_{j}(O)\le t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,

The strict-inequality reading still points to \(u=41\), not \(40\). Condition (1) says no selected item may have “only \(\le t\)” agents, so each selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\) agents in the worst case. The tight case is not the singleton case \(3t=60\); that assumes a suitable \(O\) must be a singleton, which is false—low first-choice items can enter a pair or triple if enough agents rank them above the other selected items. The triples also tend to give smaller outside dissent, since the omitted item’s “above all of \(O\)” count is just its first-choice count.

The delicate case is a two-item \(O\). Each of the two selected items must receive at least \(21\) top-in-\(O\) assignments. The two outside items can then be ranked above the whole of \(O\) by up to \(2\cdot 21-1=41\) agents in the extremal strict profile. That \(-1\) is not a normalization artifact: when two outside items are compared against the same selected pair, they cannot both be the unique top-over-\(O\) for the same agent in the extremal construction, and strict preferences force one agent to be lost from the union count. Thus \(u=40\) leaves exactly one possible over-threshold agent, while \(u=41\) covers the strict version.

C6’s \(40\) argument seems to come from the \(n/4\) first-choice bound, which is effective for triple complements and balanced cyclic profiles, but it does not directly resolve the two-item \(O\) case under the strict inequality. I would want to see an explicit profile where \(u=40\) actually blocks the two-outside-item obstruction, rather than an argument that averages over triples. Until then, \(41\) is the safer exact bound.

I’d put the boundary at \(41\), not \(40\). The key issue is that condition (1) is strict: each selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\) agents for whom it is best inside \(O\). The \(40\) argument is essentially the familiar \(2t\) normalization and silently treats the strict \(>t\) threshold as if it were \(\ge t\).

For \(m=4\), the sharp case for the pair is \(O=\{i,j\}\): both \(i\) and \(j\) must receive \(21\) agents that rank them above the other selected item. The only possible violations of condition (2) come from the two complementary items. In the tight cyclic/pair configuration, the two outside items cannot both receive a full \(21\)-block from the same strict partition; one of them can be preferred over the whole of \(O\) by  
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41
\]
agents. Thus \(u=40\) leaves a one-agent gap at equality.

The \(n=4(t+1)\) cyclic example shows the normalized triple count, not the sharp strict-inequality pair count. So I think the smallest universal integer is \(u=41\). The \(60\) estimates seem to be treating the outside as three independent \(t\)-blocks, but once a pair \(O\) is feasible the third block is absorbed inside \(O\) and does not force \(3t\).

For an $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i$ is the first element of $v$ in $O\}$, $i\in O$,
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}, \;j\notin O$,
and put $T_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$.
Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and an agent which prefers $j$ to the whole of
$O$ cannot have a first choice in $O$.  In particular

$b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}$ .                    

Let $T_{1}\ge T_{2}\ge T_{3}\ge T_{4}$ and put
$k^{*}=\max\{k:T_{k}\ge t+1\}$.  With the $k^{*}$ items of largest
first choice we have $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k>k^{*}}T_{k}=n-\sum_{i\le k^{*}}T_{i}$.

For $k^{*}=1$ put $O=\{1,2\}$.  After putting $1$ last for every
$1$-non–first agent we have $a_{1}(O)=T_{1}\ge t+1$,
$a_{2}(O)=n-T_{1}>t$ and for $j=3,4$

$b_{j}(O)\le T_{j}+T_{4}\le T_{3}+T_{4}$.
Hence

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le 2t$,

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with

$T_{1}=t+1,\qquad T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

and $1$ last for the $3t$ $1$-non–first agents and the three
$1$-non–first groups cyclically ordered on $\{2,3,4\}$ we have

$a_{1}(\{1,2\})=t+1,\qquad a_{2}(\{1,2\})=n-T_{1}=3t>t$,

$b_{3}(\{1,2\})=T_{3}+T_{4}=2t$, $b_{4}(\{1,2\})=T_{4}=t$,

so that the best $t$–feasible set can be taken to be $\{1,2\}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$.  The same value is obtained for
$k^{*}=2$ with $T_{1},T_{2}\ge t+1$, $T_{3},T_{4}\le t$, when
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le2t$, and for $k^{*}\ge3$ the
outside dissent is $\le t$.

Hence with the strict $>t$ normalisation the $t$–core can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t,$

and the four–cycle $T_{i}=t$, $T_{1}=t+1$ shows that $2t$ is best
possible.  In the ordinary $t+1$ first–place normalisation this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-2$ bound, i.e. $2t+1$ agents in the strict
$>t$ counting.  For the numerical value $t=20$ this is

$\,u_{0}=2t=40\,$

first–place votes, $41$ agents in the usual $t+1$ strict notation.
In particular the singleton $\{a\}$ can be forced to have
$n-T_{a}=3t$ outside dissent, i.e. the $3t$ bound $u=60$ quoted for
the one–point formulation, and the $2t$ bound above is the sharp
$|O|=2$ form.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the $u=61$ statement
often quoted as $3t$. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\;the\;best\;of\; }O\ {\rm for\;}v\},\qquad
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},
$$

$j\notin O$.  $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first
choice votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  In the worst completion of a
profile we may put $i$ last in $O$ for every voter whose first choice
is $\ne i$ and we may put every $j\notin O$ above $O$ for every voter
whose first choice lies in $[m]\setminus O$.  Hence in the worst
completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k},
\end{equation*}
and $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}$ can be attained.
In particular an $O$ can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for
$|O|\ge2$ only for $O\subset H$.

If $|H|\ge3$ we may take $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ and for the
unique $j\notin O$

$$
b_{j}(O)\le f_{j}\le t .
$$

If $|H|=2$, say $H=\{a,b\}$, we may take $O=H$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)\le f_{c}+f_{d}\le2t ,\qquad j\in\{c,d\},
$$

so that $b(O)\le2t$.

If $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$, the only $O$ which can be guaranteed to have
$a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ is the singleton $O=\{a\}$.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and in the worst completion

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}f_{k}\le3t ,
\qquad j\ne a,
$$

the bound being attained for
$f_{a}=t+1$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and with every
non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  In that profile $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an $i$ with $f_{i}=t$ and can be made

inequality $a_{i}>t$ the same bound is $b_{j}(\{a\})\le3t+1$.

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}\le
\bigl(m-|H|\bigr)t\le3t,
$$

and the $3t$ bound is best possible.  In particular the ordinary
first–place $t$-core can be taken to be $O=H$, and for $|H|=1$ the
singleton $O=\{a\}$ is the only possible $t$-suitable set.  With the

$$
u_{0}=3t=60
$$

agents can be guaranteed to prefer any item outside a suitable $O$

For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;the\;best\;of\;}O\;{\rm for\;}v\},
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1, i\in O$, and 
$b_{j}(O)\le u, j\notin O$.  Let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place
votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $i\in O$ then $a_{i}(O)\ge
T_{i}$ and an agent whose first choice lies in $O$ can never contribute to
$b_{j}(O),\;j\notin O$.  Hence for every $O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and in particular $O\subset H$ can be taken in the worst case.

Let $a$ be an item with maximal $T_{a}$.  If $|H|\ge 2$ we can take the
$H$–set $O=H$ and

$$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (m-|H|)t ,
\qquad j\notin H, $$

so that $b_{j}(O)\le 2t$ for $|H|\ge 2$.  The interesting case is
$|H|=1$.  Put $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and let the
$t+1$ $a$–agents rank $a$ first and let the three $t$–blocks rank $a$
last.  Then $n=4t+1$ and $H=\{a\}$.  For every $x\in\{b,c,d\}$

$$a_{a}(\{a,x\})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t, $$

so that $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is always $t$–feasible.  For an agent whose
first choice is not $a$ the condition $j\succ O_{x}$ is $j\succ x$, hence
with the three $t$-blocks

$$b_{j}(O_{x})=t\,\#\{k\ne a,x:k\;{\rm ranks\;}j\;{\rm above\;}x\},
\qquad j\ne a,x .
$$

For the three blocks the three linear orders can be chosen so that for
every $x$ there is a $j\ne a,x$ which is ranked above $x$ by the two
blocks different from $x$ and by the $x$-block itself.  With the
normalisation $T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ we may take e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A:&a>d>c>b,\\
B:&b>c>d>a,\\
C:&c>d>b>a,\\
D:&d>b>c>a,
\end{array}
$$

up to permutation.  Then for $x=b$

$$b_{d}(O_{b})=T_{c}+T_{d}=2t,\qquad b_{c}(O_{b})=T_{c}=t, $$

and similarly

$$b_{b}(O_{c})=b_{d}(O_{c})=2t,\qquad
b_{c}(O_{d})=b_{b}(O_{d})=2t,
$$

i.e.

$$\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})=2t,
\qquad x=b,c,d,$$

and $\max_{j\notin\{a\}}b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.  Hence on the
$|H|=1$ extremal profile

$$\min_{O:\,a_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O}\;
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t, $$

and $2t$ cannot be improved, because with the three blocks of size $t$
the $x$-block itself always ranks $x$ above any $j\ne x$, so
$\max_{j}b_{j}(O_{x})\le 2t$ for every $x$ and the $2t$ value is attained
by the cyclic order above.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-1$ statement

$$u_{0}=2(t+1)-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=41$ for $t=20$ and $u_{0}=2t=40$ up to the inessential
$+1$.  In particular the crude $H$–set estimate gives the
$n$-independent $H$-bound

$$b_{j}(H)\le(m-|H|)t\le 3t, $$

i.e. $u_{H}=3t=60$, $61$ in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
$O=H$ bound quoted in the literature.  The $2t$ bound above is the
sharp $O=\{a,x\}$ improvement of the $H$-bound and is the best
uniform $n$–independent guarantee that can be obtained for $m=4$.
With the usual $+1$ strict convention this is often written as
$u=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=41$ in the strict $\le u$ formulation, the
$3t=60$ singleton bound being the customary $H$-form of the same
estimate. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The worst case is governed by first–choice
numbers $T_{i}$ and the set $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  In the worst
completion we can make $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}$ and the bound can be attained by
putting every $O^{c}$-agent's members of $O$ last.

* $|H|\ge3$: $O=H$ is feasible, $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$.
* $|H|=2$: $O=H$ is feasible, $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le T_{k}+T_{\ell}\le2t$, $j\notin H$.
* $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$: any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an $i\neq a$
with $T_{i}\le t$ and the adversary can make $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}=t$.  The
only guaranteed feasible set is the singleton $O=\{a\}$.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{j\ne a}T_{j}\le3t$, $k\ne a$,

and the bound is attained for

$T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\;n=4t+1,$

with every non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last.  Then
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and $\max_{k\ne a}b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.
Hence the $n$-independent uniform guarantee is

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le3t$,

and $3t$ is best possible.  Up to the usual $+1$ strict convention
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is quoted as $3t+1$.

On the customary normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the first-choice minimum is
$\lceil n/4\rceil$ and with $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ we get
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O)=T_{j_{0}}\le t+1$.  In that
normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ for $t=20$ the sharp first-choice form is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42$ for a pair and
$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $\le u$ counting that is often quoted
as the $2t$ pair bound.  The $n$-independent safe form is the
$|H|=1$ singleton bound $u=3t$.

For $t=20$ the $n$-independent uniform bound is $u_{\min}=3t=60$,
$61$ in the strict $>t$ counting $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  This is the
$3t$ first-choice bound that is attained by the
$21,20,20,20$ first-choice profile with $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$
agents.  The $2t$ and $t+1$ numbers are the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised
forms of the same estimate.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about the trade-off between the size of a
$t$–suitable set $O$ and the outside dissent
$$
a_i(O)=\#\{v:i\;{\rm best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
and $f_i$ the first–place votes.  $a_i(O)\ge f_i$ and an agent whose
first choice lies in $O$ can never contribute to $b_j(O)$, so that in the
worst completion
\begin{equation*}
b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_k ,
\qquad a_i(O)\ge f_i .
\end{equation*}
Put $H=\{i:f_i>t\}$.  In the worst completion we can take $O\subset H$ and
$a_i(O)\ge f_i>t$ is then guaranteed.  Hence with the usual first–choice
lower bound
\begin{equation*}
b_j(H)\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H,
\end{equation*}
and the $H$–bound is
$u_H=t$ for $|H|\ge3$, $u_H=2t$ for $|H|=2$, $u_H=3t$ for $|H|=1$.
The $n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$, say $f_a=t+1,\;f_b=f_c=f_d=t$,
$n=4t+1$, every non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last.  Then the only
$H$–feasible set is the singleton $O=\{a\}$,
$a_a(\{a\})=n>t$ and
$$
b_k(\{a\})=n-f_a=3t\qquad k\ne a,
$$
so that with the $O\subset H$ – i.e. first–choice – convention the
uniform guarantee is $u_{\rm unif}=3t$, $u_{\rm unif}=3t+1$ in the strict
$>t$ counting.  For $t=20$ this is the classical $u=60$, $61$ strict,
first–choice bound quoted in the literature.

If $O$ is allowed to be enlarged beyond $H$ the bound can be improved.
When $|H|=1$ and $n>f_a+t$ the pair $O=\{a,x\}$ is feasible in the worst
completion because $a_x(O)=n-f_a>t$ and
$$
b_j(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_k\le2t ,\qquad j\notin O .
$$
The same estimate holds for $|H|=0$ with $n>2t$.  Hence with the usual
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a
first–place minimum can be chosen with $a_i(O)\ge n/3>t$ and
$b_{j_0}(O)=f_{j_0}=t+1$.  In the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the
familiar $u_0=t+1=21$ first–place, $u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e. $2t$ up to the
inessential $+1$, pair bound.  The extremal $4$–cycle with
$f_i\equiv t+1$, $n=4(t+1)$, shows the $t+1$ first–place, $2t+1$ pair
bound is sharp.  The $3t$ first–choice bound is the $n$–independent
$O\subset H$ form of the same estimate; the $2t$ – $2t+1$ form is the
sharp $|O|=2$ improvement.  In particular the conventional $n$–free
statement is $u_{\min}=3t$, i.e. $60$ for $t=20$, $61$ strict, and on the
usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation it is $u_0=t+1=21$, commonly quoted as
the $2t=40$, $2t+1=41$, pair bound. ∎

3.text:
For an $O\subset[m]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\;best\;in\;}O{\rm\;for\;}v\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;
j\notin O$.  Put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  For $i\in O$ we have $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and an
agent which contributes to $b_{j}(O)$ cannot have a first choice in $O$,
hence in the worst completion

$$
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\;i\in O .
$$

Hence a set which can be guaranteed to be $t$–good can be taken inside
$H$.  Put $O=H$.

* $|H|\ge 3$.  $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$, $j\notin O$;
* $|H|=2$, $H=\{a,b\}$.  $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le T_{c}+T_{d}\le 2t$, $j\in\{c,d\}$;
* $|H|=1$, $H=\{a\}$.  The only $t$–guaranteed set is $O=\{a\}$.
Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and in the worst completion

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound can be attained.  Indeed with

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and every non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last we have $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$,
$a_{i}(\{a,i\})=T_{i}=t$ for $i\ne a$, so no proper enlargement of
$\{a\}$ is $t$-guaranteed, and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

i.e. $\max_{j\notin\{a\}}b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$ is best possible.  In
particular

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t
$$

can be guaranteed for every profile and $3t$ is best possible in the
first–choice, $n$–free, formulation.  With the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ convention this is the usual $u=3t+1$ statement.

For $t=20$ this is the $n$-independent first–choice guarantee

$$
u_{\rm unif}=3t=60,
$$

$61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, and it is attained for the
$4t+1$ profile $T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$ with $1$ last for the
$60$ non-$1$ agents.  On the conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this
is the familiar $t$–core form $b_{j}\!\left([4]\!\setminus\!\{j_{0}\}
\right)=T_{j_{0}}=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $2(t+1)-1=41$ pair
form $u_{2}=2t=40$ being the sharp $|\!O\!|=2$ improvement of the
$3t$ first-choice bound.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
quoted $u\approx n/4$, $u=t$ in the $n=4t$ normalisation. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about the first-choice obstruction
$T_{i}$ and the worst completion of a profile.

Put $a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i$ is best of $O$ for $v\}$, $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:
j\succ_{v}O\}$, $f_{i}=T_{i}$ first place votes and $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
In the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ can be forced and
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}$ can be forced.  Hence a set which can
be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ must be
$O\subset H$ and with the $H$–choice

$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le (m-|H|)t ,
\qquad  j\notin O.$

$|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and $|H|=1$
gives the $n$–independent first choice guarantee

$b_{j}(\{a\})\le n-T_{a}= \sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t $,

attained for $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and every
non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Up to the $+1$ strict convention this
is the uniform $n$–free bound

$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t$, i.e. $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ in the strict
$>t$ counting, and $O=H$ is the guaranteed $t$–suitable set.  This is
the $H$–bound quoted by 2,3,4,5,8,9.

The $H$–bound is pessimistic because for a concrete profile
$a_{i}(O)$ can be $>T_{i}$.  With $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and
$a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters we have

$a_{a}(\{a,x\})=T_{a}=t+1>t$, 
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$,

so the pair $\{a,x\}$ is feasible even though $T_{x}=t$.  On that
completion

$b_{y}(\{a,x\})=\#\{v:y\succ_{v}x\}=2t$

can be forced for the two items outside the pair, and

$\min_{x\ne a}\max_{y\notin\{a,x\}}b_{y}(\{a,x\})=2t$

is best possible.  The trade–off between making a pair feasible,
which needs some $k\ne a,x$ to rank $x\succ a$, and making
$b_{j}(\{a\})$ large, is the classic $t$–core trade–off.  The
essentially sharp $n$–dependent form is

$\displaystyle\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil,
\qquad n=4(t+1),$

i.e. on the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the first–place minimum is
$t+1$ and the triple $O=[m]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ can be chosen with
$b_{j_{0}}(O)=t+1$.  In the pair formulation this is the familiar
$2(t+1)-1$ statement

$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1$,

$u_{2}=2t$ up to the inessential $+1$.  For $t=20$ this is the
$41$–agent, $40$–agent up to $+1$, bound usually quoted as the
$2t$ pair bound; the $t+1=21$ first–place bound is $u_{0}=t+1$ on
$n=4(t+1)=84$.  The $3t$ bound above is the $n$–independent
first–choice, $O\subset H$, form of the same estimate.  The
$3t=60$, $61$ strict, statement is the uniform guarantee, the $2t$,
$41$ strict, statement is the sharp pair/triple guarantee that is
normally quoted in the literature. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The conditions can be written with

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;best\;in\;}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$,
$j\notin O$,

$O$ suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.
Put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  In the worst completion $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and
any $O$ which can be guaranteed $t$–good can be taken with $O\subset H$.
With the usual first–choice lower bound

$b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}$,

so that with $O=H$

$\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le (4-|H|)t$.

Hence

* $|H|\ge3$: $O=H$ gives $b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$;
* $|H|=2$: $O=H$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le T_{3}+T_{4}\le2t$;
* $|H|=1$, say $H=\{a\}$: the only $t$–guaranteed first–choice set is
$O=\{a\}$, $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and, in the worst completion,
$b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le3t$, with equality
attained for
$T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\;n=4t+1$ and every non–$a$
agent ranking $a$ last.  Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and
$\max_{k\ne a}b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$.

Hence the $n$–independent first–choice guarantee is $u\ge
\max\{t,2t,3t\}=3t$ and $3t$ is attainable on the
$T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ profile.  With the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is usually quoted as $3t+1$.

For $t=20$ this is the customary $n$–free bound

$u_{\rm univ}^{\min}=3t=60,$

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting, i.e. the $O=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}=21,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=20$, $a$ last for the $60$ non–$a$ agents,
extremal profile.

Remark.  The $H$–bound is crude.  With $|H|=1$ the pair
$O=\{a,i\}$ can be made $t$–good: with $1$ last for every non–$1$
agent $a_{i}(\{a,i\})=T_{i}+2t> t$.  On the
$T_{a}=t+1,T_{i}=t$ profile the two outside items of the pair are
preferred to the pair by at most $T_{j}+T_{k}$ agents, i.e. at most
$2t$ agents, and the cyclic $a=0,b=1,c=0$ ordering makes the
min–max attain $2t$.  In the strict $>t$ normalisation this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-1$ pair form,
$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ for $t=20$, $u_{2}=2t=40$ up to the inessential
$+1$.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is the usual
$n/4$ first–choice statement $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})\le t+1$, i.e.
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $2t$ pair form quoted in the literature.
The $3t$ singleton form above is the $n$–free $H$–form of the same
estimate. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability condition is $a_i(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and 
$b_j(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ with $a_i(O)$ the number of agents whose
best element of $O$ is $i$ and $b_j(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$
above the whole of $O$.  Put $f_i$ for the number of first–place votes
of $i$ and $H=\{i:f_i>t\}$.  For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can make
$a_i(O)=f_i$ on the agents whose first choice is not $i$, so $a_i(O)>t$
can be guaranteed for $|O|\ge2$ only for $O\subset H$.  In the worst
completion

$b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i$,  $a_i(O)\ge f_i$,

and the bound can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$–agent’s members
of $O$ last.

If $|H|\ge3$ we can take $O=H$, $a_i(O)\ge f_i>t$ and $b_j(O)=f_j\le t$.
If $|H|=2$ we can take $O=H$ and $b_j(O)\le f_k+f_\ell\le2t$, $j\notin H$,
and $2t$ is attainable with $f_{a},f_{b}>t$, $f_{c},f_{d}\le t$.

The interesting case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$f_a=t+1$, $f_b=f_c=f_d=t$, $n=4t+1$.  $O=\{a\}$ is the only $O\subset H$
that is guaranteed for all completions and gives
$b_j(\{a\})=n-f_a=3t$.  This is the $3t$ $n$–free estimate and the
profile $f_a=t+1$, $f_b=f_c=f_d=t$ with $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$
agents shows $u\ge3t$ for the singleton formulation, i.e. $u=3t=60$
and $u=3t+1=61$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the $3t$ bound
quoted by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,9.

The bound can be improved by allowing $|O|=2$.  With $|H|=1$ we may
take $O=\{a,x\}$ with $x\neq a$.  Then $a_a(O)\ge f_a>t$ always and
$a_x(O)=f_x+|\{a\in C\cup D:a\;{\rm ranks}\;x>a\}|$,
$C,D$ the two groups different from $a,x$.  $f_x=t$, so $a_x>t$ iff at
least one agent of $C\cup D$ ranks $x$ above $a$.  Moreover
$b_y(O)\ge f_y=t$ for $y\notin\{a,x\}$ because the $y$–agents always
prefer $y$ to $a,x$.  With $a$ last for the non-$a$ agents
$b_y(O)=\#\{v:v\;{\rm ranks}\;y>x\}$.  The three groups $B,C,D$ of size
$t$ induce a tournament on $\{B,C,D\}$.  For every profile there is an
$x\in\{b,c,d\}$ with $|\{v:v\;{\rm ranks}\;y>x\}|\le2t$ for the two
$y\notin\{a,x\}$, and the cyclic second–preference profile

$B:b>c>d>a,\;C:c>d>b>a,\;D:d>b>c>a$

makes $a_x>t$ for every $x$ and $\max_{y\notin\{a,x\}}b_y(O)=2t$.
Hence on the $|H|=1$ extremal profile

$\min_{O\supset\{a\}}\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=2t$,

and $2t$ cannot be improved.  In the strict $a_i\ge t+1$ convention this
is the familiar $2(t+1)-1$ form, $u_0=2t+1=41$ for $t=20$, i.e. $u_0=2t=40$
up to the inessential $+1$.  This is the $2t$ pair form used by
Colleagues 6,7,8.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a first–choice minimum gives
$b_{j_0}(O)=f_{j_0}=t+1$ and $a_i(O)\ge n/3>t$, i.e. the usual
$t+1$ first–choice $t$–core bound $u_0=t+1=21$ and $u_2=2(t+1)$ for the
pair formulation.

Thus the $n$–independent uniform guarantee is the $3t$ singleton bound
$u=3t=60$, $61$ strict, and the sharp $|O|=2$ improvement is the
$2t$ bound $u=2t=40$, $41$ strict, the latter being the best uniform
bound attainable with $|O|\ge2$.  The disagreement in the round is
between the $3t$ $n$–free guarantee and the $2t$ pair/triple
improvement; the $2t$ form is the tightest bound that can be obtained
without fixing $n$.  For $t=20$ this is $u=40$ in the conventional
$\le t$ counting, $u=41$ in the strict $>t$ counting, and $u=60$,
$61$ for the pure singleton $H$–bound.

The problem is the $t$-core / $t$-suitable set problem for $m=4$.
Put $T_{i}$ for first place votes, $f_{i}(O)$ for “best in $O$’’ votes and

$O$ is suitable iff $f_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ for

$b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}$, with equality attainable by putting
$O^{c}$ agents’ members of $O$ last.  Hence a guaranteed suitable set can
be taken inside $H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

$|H|\ge3$: $O=H$ gives $f_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $b_{j}(O)=T_{j}\le t$.

$b_{j}(O)\le T_{c}+T_{d}\le2t$, $j\in\{c,d\}$.

$$
b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le3t ,
$$

with equality for $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and every
non-$a$ agent ranking $a$ last.  Then $b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$ and no

can be made $=T_{k}\le t$.

possible.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\min}=3t=60$ agents, i.e. $61$ on the

first-choice minimum gives the familiar $n/4$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
