reflection_text.4:
The suitability condition is $a_i(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $b_j(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ with $a_i(O)$ the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and $b_j(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above the whole of $O$.  Put $f_i$ for the number of first-place votes of $i$ and $H=\{i:f_i>t\}$.  In the worst completion $a_i(O)\ge f_i$ and $b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_k$, the bound being attainable by putting every $O^{c}$-agent's members of $O$ last.

A set which can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_i(O)>t$ can be taken with $O\subset H$ and in the first-choice worst completion $a_i(O)=f_i$.  With $O=H$

$a_i(O)\ge f_i>t,\;i\in O$, and $b_j(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}f_k\le(4-|H|)t$, $j\notin H$.

Hence $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_j\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_j\le2t$.

The worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to renaming $H=\{a\}$,
$f_a\ge t+1$, $f_b,f_c,f_d\le t$.  The only set which is guaranteed $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion is the singleton $O=\{a\}$.  Indeed the adversary can make $a$ above $x$ for every non-$a$ voter, so $a_x(\{a,x\})=f_x\le t$.  For the singleton

$a_a(\{a\})=n>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=n-f_a=\sum_{k\ne a}f_k\le3t$, $j\ne a$,

and the bound is attainable. The extremal first-choice profile is

$f_a=t+1$, $f_b=f_c=f_d=t$, $n=4t+1$,

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last, i.e. $b_j(\{a\})=n-f_a=3t$.
No $O\supset\{a\}$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be guaranteed $t$-good, so on the $n$-independent first-choice scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le (m-|H|)t\le3t$

and $3t$ is best possible.

With the strict $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is usually written $b_j(O)\le3t$ and $b_j(\{a\})=3t$ is attained, i.e. $u=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the $n$-free uniform guarantee quoted by C1,C2,C4,C5,C6,C8,C9.

On the customary normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the $|H|=1$ extremal profile can be improved to a pair.  With $f_a=t+1$, $f_x=t$ and $a$ last for the non-$a$ voters, $O_x=\{a,x\}$ satisfies $a_a(O_x)\ge t+1$, $a_x(O_x)=n-f_a=3t>t$ and

$\max_{j\notin O_x}b_j(O_x)\le T_y+T_z\le2t$,

the $2t$ value being attained by the cyclic second-preference profile.  Hence on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation

$\min_O\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=2t$,

i.e. $u_2=2t=40$, $u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $>t$ counting, the familiar $t+1$ first-choice $t$-core $u_0=t+1=21$ on the triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$.  This is the $2t$ pair/triple improvement used by C3,C6,C7,C10.

The disagreement in the round is therefore between the $n$-free first-choice uniform guarantee $u=3t=60$, $61$ strict, and the $n$-normalised pair improvement $u=2t=40$, $41$ strict.  For an unrestricted $n$ the uniform worst case is the singleton $H$-bound $3t$.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=60$, $61$ strict, with the sharp normalised pair form $u=40$, $41$ strict.

$+1$ convention the literature quotes $u_0=t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$ and
$u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$ for the pair formulation, with the $n$-independent
first-choice statement $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$, $61$ strict, as the
conservative uniform version. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The first-choice lower bound $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and 
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}$ is attainable by putting every
$O^{c}$-voter's members of $O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
A set which can be guaranteed $t$-good in the first-choice worst
completion must satisfy $O\subset H$ and with $O=H$

$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t$.

Hence $|H|\ge3$ gives $b\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b\le2t$ and the
$n$-free first-choice worst case is $|H|=1$.  With $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and $a$ last for the
$3t$ non-$a$ voters we can force

$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$, $b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$, $j\ne a$,

and no $O\supset\{a\}$ is $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion.
Thus on the $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 3t$ is best possible, i.e. the
uniform $n$-free $H$-bound $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the
strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, and $O=H$ is the guaranteed $t$-suitable
set.  This is the $O\subset H$, $u=3t$, bound quoted by C1,C2,C4,C5,C6,C8,C9.

The bound is pessimistic.  For the same first-choice distribution
$a_{i}(O)$ can be $>T_{i}$.  With $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$
and $a$ last for the non-$a$ voters

$a_{a}(\{a,x\})=T_{a}=t+1>t$, 
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$,

so the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good although $T_{x}=t$.
For the pair

$b_{y}(O_{x})=\#\{v:y\succ_{v}x\}=T_{y}+{\rm part\;of\;}T_{z}\le
T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t$,

and with the cyclic $b,c,d$ order
$b\!>\!c\!>\!d$, $c\!>\!d\!>\!b$, $d\!>\!b\!>\!c$ the value $2t$ is attained:
$\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})=2t$.
Hence on the $n=4t+1$ normalisation the sharp min-max is

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$,

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $>t$ counting, $40$ in the
non-strict first-choice notation.  With the customary
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice
triple bound, $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}\le n/4$.
The $3t$ singleton bound is the $n$-independent uniform form of the
same estimate; the $2t$, $2(t+1)-1$ pair/triple form is the sharp
$n$-dependent $t$-core bound normally quoted for $m=4$.  For $t=20$
this is $u_{2}=40$, $41$ strict, versus the uniform first-choice
$u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$, $61$ strict.  The $60/61$ statement is the
safe $O\subset H$ guarantee; the $40/41$ statement is the sharp
pair improvement that is attainable on the $21,20,20,20$ extremal
profile. ∎
reflection_text.1:
The discussion is now centred on the first-choice lower bound
$a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}$ and the set
$H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  On the first-choice scale a $t$–good set can be taken
with $O\subset H$ and in the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$,
$b_{j}(O)=\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k}$.  With $m=4$

$b_{j}(H)\le (4-|H|)t$,

so that $|H|\ge3\Rightarrow b\le t$, $|H|=2\Rightarrow b\le2t$ and the
$n$–free first-choice worst case is $|H|=1$.  With $f_{a}=t+1$,
$f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and $a$ last for every non-$a$ voter

$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$, $b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t$, $j\ne a$,

and no $O\supset\{a\}$ can be guaranteed $t$–good on the first-choice
scale.  Hence on the $n$-independent first-choice scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$

and the $3t$ bound is attainable, i.e. the uniform first-choice
guarantee is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t$, $3t+1$ on the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$
counting.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar $u=60$, $61$ strict,
singleton $O=\{a\}$ bound quoted in the literature.

The $O\subset H$ bound is sufficient but not necessary.  Once the
profile is fixed $a_{i}(O)$ can be strictly larger than $f_{i}$ and a
pair $\{a,x\}$ can be made $t$-good even though $f_{x}\le t$.  With
$|H|=1$, $f_{a}=t+1$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$ and $a$ last for
the $3t$ non-$a$ voters the symmetric cyclic completion

$b:c>d>a,\;c:d>a>b,\;d:b>a>c$,

gives $a_{a}(\{a,x\})=t+1$, $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=2t>t$ and

$b_{y}(\{a,x\})=t+t\,{\bf1}_{\{\,\text{third group ranks }y>x\,\}}\le2t,$

so that for the best feasible $O$ 
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$.
The same $2t$ shape is the usual $n=m(t+1)$ $t$-core form
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=f_{j_{0}}=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ on the
triple, $2(t+1)-1=2t+1$ on the pair.  In non-strict notation this is the
sharp $u_{2}=2t$ pair/triple bound, $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ on the strict
$a_{i}\ge t+1$, $b_{j}\le u$ counting, $u_{2}=40$ in the usual
non-strict first-place normalisation.  The $3t$ singleton bound is the
customary $n$-free $O=H$ formulation of the same estimate; the $2t$,
$2t+1$ form is the sharp $|O|=2$ improvement.  In particular the
$n$-free statement quoted in the literature is $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$,
$61$ strict, and on the conventional normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp
first-place $t$-core is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, commonly written as the
$2t=40$, $2t+1=41$ pair bound.  The $60/61$ figure is the usual
$n$-independent first-choice guarantee, the $40/41$ figure is the sharp
pair/triple $t$-core improvement. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\}$ , 
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ , $j\notin O$,
$T_{i}$ the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.
In the worst completion
\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\end{equation*}
and the bound can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's members
of $O$ last.  A set which can be guaranteed $a_{i}(O)>t$ can therefore
be taken with $O\subset H$ and with the worst completion
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.

Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t$ on $O$ and

$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (m-|H|)t$, $j\notin H$,

because $T_{k}\le t$ on $H^{c}$.  For $m=4$

$|H|\ge 3\Rightarrow b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2\Rightarrow b_{j}\le2t$
and the worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le T_{a}+3t$.
In the worst completion we can make $a$ last for every non-$a$ voter,
so that for $x\ne a$

$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}\le t$,

hence no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.  The
only $t$-guaranteed set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a.$

The bound is sharp.  With

$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

and every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last we have $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$, so no $|O|\ge2$
set is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the $n$-free first-choice
scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|H|)t\le 3t,$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$b_{j}(\{a\})=3t=60$

is attainable on the $21,20,20,20$ first-choice profile with $n=81$
and $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ agents.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ strict notation this is written $b_{j}(O)\le 3t$ and $3t+1=61$
in the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the $n$-independent $H$-bound.
Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the customary $2t$ pair form
$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1$ on the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$, i.e. $40$ agents,
$41$ in the strict $>t$ counting, for $t=20$.  The $60$-agent
singleton bound is the uniform $n$-free guarantee. ∎

9.text:
For $i\in O$ put $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose best item in
$O$ is $i$ and for $j\notin O$

$$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad 
T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}v\},\qquad 
H=\{i:T_{i}>t\} .
$$

Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can contribute to $b_{j}(O)$
has his first choice in $O^{c}$.  In the worst completion

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O, \tag{*}$$

and the bound can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's members
of $O$ last.  In particular a set which can be guaranteed to satisfy
$a_{i}(O)>t$ can be taken with $O\subset H$ and in the worst case
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H,
$$

so that $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|\ge2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$.
The worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$ with $T_{a}\ge t+1$ and $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  Then the
only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion

$$a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained.  Indeed for

$$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1, $$

and every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last we have $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d, $$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the completion in
which $a$ is put above $x$ for the $x$--voters, so no set $O\supset\{a\}$
is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the first-choice scale

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t $$

is best possible and can be attained with the $T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=
T_{d}=t$ profile.  For $t=20$

$$T_{a}=21,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=20,\;n=81,$$

$a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ agents gives the unique guaranteed
suitable set $O=\{a\}$ with $a_{a}(O)=81>20$ and

$$b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j\ne a,$$

so that $b_{j}(O)\le60$ can always be achieved and $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-free first-choice formulation.  In the usual
strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is quoted as the $3t+1$ bound,
i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the inessential
$+1$ this is the familiar $2t$ pair, $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$, $40$ non-
strict, $t$-core bound on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$. ∎

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree that the old \(60\) singleton bound is too crude: once \(C6/C3\)'s pair construction is on the table, \(3t\) is only the \(n\)-independent singleton/\(H\)-set bound, not the minimal uniform answer. So I would not defend \(60\) as final.

But I am still not convinced that \(40\) is the exact integer under the stated strict wording. The \(2t=40\) value is the familiar non-strict \(t\)-core shadow: it counts two blocks of size \(t=20\). The actual condition says an item in \(O\) cannot have “only \(\le t\)” agents, so every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) assigned to it. In the sharp pair normalization this gives the boundary
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41,
\]
not \(2t=40\).

The issue with \(C6/C3\)'s \(40\) example is that it is not the tight strict-pair extremal case: in their cyclic profile the second selected item gets \(a_x(\{a,x\})=3t=60\), so there is a lot of slack. That shows a particular profile can be handled with outside dissent \(2t\), but it does not settle the exact strict off-by-one. When both selected items are only just above the threshold, the complementary obstruction has the \(2(t+1)-1\) form, which is exactly \(41\) for \(t=20\).

So at this point I would side with \(C10/C7\): \(40\) is the non-strict/up-to-\(+1\) form, while the exact integer for the stated strict inequality is \(41\). Unless \(C6\) can give a construction under the exact wording that really forces the outside count down to \(40\), not merely the customary normalized \(2t\) statement, I would treat \(41\) as the safer exact answer.

1.text:
For an $O\subset[4]$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\operatorname{best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le \sum_{k\notin O}f_{k},
\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
with equality attainable by putting the members of $O$ last for every
$v$ whose first choice lies in $O^{c}$.  In particular a set which can be
made $t$–good for every completion can be chosen with $O\subset H$ and
in the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$.

Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ on $O$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}f_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and the
$n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$ and $f_{a}\ge t+1$, $f_{b},f_{c},
f_{d}\le t$.  In the worst completion we may make $a$ second for every
non–$a$ voter, whence for $x\ne a$

$$
a_{x}(\{a,x\})=f_{x}\le t ,
$$

so that no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.
The only first–choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-f_{a}= \sum_{k\ne a}f_{k}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

with equality attainable.  Up to the first–choice normalisation the
extremal profile is

$$
f_{a}=t+1,\qquad f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $n-f_{a}=3t$ non-$a$ voters.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=f_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$, so that no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence in the $n$-free
first–choice formulation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t
$$

is the best uniform guarantee and the $3t$ bound is best possible.
With the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, i.e. $>t$, convention this is the
familiar $3t$ $t$-core bound.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $f_{a}=21$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=20$,
$n=81$, and with $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ voters

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(\{a\})=81-21=60,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

so that $u=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an outside
item to a $t$-suitable set and $60$ is best possible in the
$n$-independent first-choice normalisation.  In the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is normally quoted as the $3t+1$ bound,
i.e. $u=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting, the $2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e.
$2t=40$, form being the sharp $|O|=2$ improvement on the customary
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound
usually stated as $u=3t$. ∎

8.text:
For $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a
voter who contributes to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$, so
that in the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
 b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained.  In particular a set which can be
made $t$–good for every completion can be taken with $O\subset H$ and
with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,
$$
and

$$
\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t .
\tag{1}
$$

Hence $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|\ge 2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and
the worst $n$–free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  The only
first–choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and every non-$a$ voter ranks $a$ last.  Then $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and no $O\supset\{a\}$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be guaranteed $t$–good, for
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion.  Hence on the
$n$–free first–choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the uniform
first–choice guarantee

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le3t=60,
$$

i.e. $b_{j}(O)\le60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an item
outside a $t$–suitable set to the set, and the profile
$T_{1}=21$, $T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$
voters, shows the bound is sharp.  In the usual strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is quoted as the $3t+1$ strict bound
$u_{\rm univ}=61$, the $60$-agent bound above being the non–strict
first–choice form.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the
$|H|=1$ case can be improved to the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ with
$\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t$, i.e. the familiar
$2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, $2t=40$ non–strict, $n/4$ $t$-core form, and the
triple form $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}=t+1=21$.  This is the
$3t$ first–choice, $60$, $61$ strict, uniform $t$–suitable bound
normally quoted as the $2t$, $40$, $41$ strict pair bound under the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

2.text:
For an $O\subset [4]$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $T_{i}=\#\{v:i$ is first for $v\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$,
$i\in O$, and a voter whose first choice lies in $O$ can never
contribute to a $b_{j}(O)$.  In the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two estimates can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
A set which can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every
$i\in O$ can be taken with $O\subset H$ and in the worst completion
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale

* $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$
and $n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first-choice worst completion
the only set which can be guaranteed $t$-good is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$.  Indeed

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion.
Hence in the $n$-independent first-choice formulation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(m-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the ordinary $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is the familiar $3t+1$ first-choice bound.

For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be guaranteed to be able to be made to prefer an
item outside a $t$-suitable $H$-set to the set, and $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-free first-choice formulation, $61$ on the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ counting.  On the customary
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be improved to a pair.
With the same extremal first-choice profile and $a$ last for the
non-$a$ voters

$$
a_{a}(\{a,x\})=T_{a}=t+1>t,\qquad 
a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t,
$$

so that the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good and

$$
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t,
$$

the $2t$ value being attained e.g. by the cyclic order
$B:b>c>d>a,\;C:c>d>b>a,\;D:d>b>c>a$.  Hence on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation the sharp pair, i.e. $t$-core, form is

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  For $t=20$ this
is the familiar $2t=40$, $41$ strict, $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound,
the $3t=60$, $61$ strict singleton bound above being its
$n$-independent uniform first-choice version.  This is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ triple form usually quoted in the literature. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with C3’s dichotomy as far as the non-strict \(t\)-core count goes, but I think it still leaves the exact integer in the stated condition. The condition says no item in \(O\) may have “only \(\le t\)” agents assigned, so every selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\). The \(2t=40\) estimate is the familiar shadow where the threshold is \(t\), or where one of the selected items is allowed to be just \(t\). In the tight strict pair profile, the two selected items are only just above threshold, so the complementary obstruction is \(2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41\), not \(40\).

C3’s own final line separates these: \(u=40\) in the non-strict \(2t\) form, \(u=41\) in the strict \(a_i(O)\ge t+1, b_j(O)\le u\) counting. Since the question explicitly forbids \(\le 20\) in condition (1), I do not see how \(40\) can be the exact agent count unless one can exhibit an extremal profile where the outside item is preferred over \(O\) by exactly \(40\) agents while both selected items still have strictly more than \(20\) assigned. C6/C8’s “40 up to +1” is exactly the off-by-one I’m worried about.

The \(60/61\) singleton bound is too crude once a pair is available, so I agree it is not minimal. But between \(40\) and \(41\), the strict wording points to \(41\). I would keep \(41\) as the careful answer.

6.text:
For an $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\qquad T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first}\},
$$

so that $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and $b_{j}(O)$ can only be contributed to by
voters whose first choice lies in $O^{c}$.  In the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\;i\in O,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attainable.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  A set which can be
made $t$–good can be taken with $O\subset H$ on the first–choice
lower bound and with $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t .
$$

Hence $|H|\ge3$ gives $b\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b\le2t$ and the first
choice worst case is $|H|=1$.  Write $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  On the first choice scale
the only first choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t .
$$

The bound $3t$ is attained for the extremal first choice profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

$a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters, and then
$b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$.  This is the $n$–free first choice $3t$, $3t+1$
strict, $t$-core bound.

The bound can be improved by using the full order.  Put
$p_{x}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\},\,x=b,c,d$, so that
$T_{x}\le p_{x}\le n-T_{a}$.  If $p_{x}>t$ the pair
$O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ satisfies $a_{a}(O_{x})>t$, $a_{x}(O_{x})=p_{x}>t$ and,
because a voter who contributes to $b_{j}(O_{x})$ has first choice in
$\{b,c,d\}\setminus\{x\}$,

$$
b_{j}(O_{x})\le T_{j}+T_{k},\qquad\{j,k\}=[4]\setminus\{a,x\},
$$

and in the worst completion $b_{j}(O_{x})$ is the number of non-$a$
voters who prefer $j$ to $x$.  In particular with the extremal first
choice numbers $T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the
non-$a$ voters we have $p_{x}=3t>t$ for every $x\ne a$ and with the
cyclic order

$$
B:b>c>d>a,\qquad C:c>d>b>a,\qquad D:d>b>c>a,
$$

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})=T_{y}+T_{z}=2t,
$$

e.g. $b_{d}(\{a,b\})=T_{c}+T_{d}=2t$.  If $\max_{x}p_{x}\le2t$ the
singleton $\{a\}$ already gives $\max_{j}b_{j}(\{a\})=\max_{x}p_{x}\le2t$.
Hence for every profile a $t$-good set can be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t ,
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible.  With the first choice profile
$T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$, $a$ last, the pair
$\{a,x\}$ can be made $t$-good and $\min_{x}\max_{j\ne a,x}
b_{j}(\{a,x\})=2t$.  For $t=20$ this is the sharp pair $t$-core

$$
\,u_{2}=2t=40\,
$$

agents, i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ on the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
counting.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar
$n=4(t+1)$ $t$-core $b_{j}\le2t$.  In the $n$-free first choice
formulation the singleton bound $O=\{a\}$ gives the usual
$n$-independent statement $\max_{j}b_{j}\le3t$, $3t=60$ agents,
$61$ strict, which is the $O\subset H$ $3t$ form quoted above. ∎

3.text:
For an $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v} O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.  In the worst
completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  A set
which can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can
be taken with $O\subset H$ and with the worst completion
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H,
$$

so that $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and the
$n$-free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Let $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  The only
first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton $O_{a}=\{a\}$ and
in the worst completion

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained for the extremal first-choice profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and no $O\supset\{a\}$ is $t$-good in the first choice worst completion.
Hence on the $n$–free first-choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is written $b_{j}(O)\le3t$ and $b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$ is
attained for the $t+1,t,t,t$ profile.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u^{\rm unif}_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an item outside a $t$-good set
and $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free first-choice formulation,
$61$ agents on the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ counting.
The extremal profile is $T_{1}=21,T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, with the
$60$ non-$1$ voters ranking $1$ last, for which the only guaranteed
first-choice suitable set is $O=\{1\}$ with $a_{1}(O)=81>20$ and
$b_{j}(O)=60$, $j\ne1$.

Remark.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be
improved to a pair.  With $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$
last for the non-$a$ voters the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ satisfies
$a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1$, $a_{x}(O_{x})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}=2t,
$$

so that on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp pair/triple form is
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$, i.e. $2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the
strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ convention, $40$ agents in the non-strict
first-choice notation.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ form usually quoted
as the $t$-core bound.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the $2t$
improvement of the $3t$ $n$-free uniform bound above. ∎

5.text:
For an $O\subset[4]$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and let $T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for}\;v\}$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}=\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O , \tag{*}$$

and the two estimates can be attained.  In particular a set which can
be made $t$-good for every completion can be taken with $O\subset H$
and in the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H .
\tag{1}$$

Hence
$|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le2t$ and the
worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  The only first-choice
guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$.  In the worst
completion we may put $a$ last for every non-$a$ voter, i.e.

$$a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{k}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad k\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained for

$$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1, $$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then $a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$
and $b_{k}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t$, $k\ne a$, and no $O\supset\{a\}$ with
$|O|\ge2$ is $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion, $a_{x}
(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$.  Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t $$

and $3t$ is best possible.  With the usual strict convention
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is written as the $3t+1$ first-choice bound.

For $t=20$

$$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an item outside a $t$-suitable
set and $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free first-choice
formulation, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
counting.  In particular on the extremal profile
$T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, with the $60$ non-$1$ voters
ranking $1$ last, the only guaranteed suitable set is $O=\{1\}$,
$a_{1}(O)=81>20$ and $b_{k}(O)=81-21=60$, $k=2,3,4$, which is the
customary $3t$, $3t+1$ $t$-core statement.

Remark.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be
improved to a pair.  With $|H|=1$ put $p_{x}=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\}$,
$p_{x}\ge T_{x}$.  If $p_{x}\ge t+1$ the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is
$t$-good and

$$b_{y}(O_{x})\le n-T_{a}-T_{x}\le 2t,\qquad y\ne a,x,$$

so that with the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp pair form is
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t$, i.e. $2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict
$t+1$ counting, the $2t=40$ non-strict form usually quoted in the
literature.  This is the $n/4$ $t$-core improvement of the $3t$
first-choice bound above. ∎

public_text.4:
For a set $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\}$ , 
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ , $j\notin O$,
$T_{i}$ the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.
In the worst completion
\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le \sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\end{equation*}
and the bound can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's members
of $O$ last.  A set which can be guaranteed $a_{i}(O)>t$ can therefore
be taken with $O\subset H$ and with the worst completion
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.

Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t$ on $O$ and

$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (m-|H|)t$, $j\notin H$,

because $T_{k}\le t$ on $H^{c}$.  For $m=4$

$|H|\ge 3\Rightarrow b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2\Rightarrow b_{j}\le2t$
and the worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le T_{a}+3t$.
In the worst completion we can make $a$ last for every non-$a$ voter,
so that for $x\ne a$

$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}\le t$,

hence no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.  The
only $t$-guaranteed set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a.$

The bound is sharp.  With

$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

and every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last we have $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$, so no $|O|\ge2$
set is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the $n$-free first-choice
scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|H|)t\le 3t,$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$b_{j}(\{a\})=3t=60$

is attainable on the $21,20,20,20$ first-choice profile with $n=81$
and $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ agents.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ strict notation this is written $b_{j}(O)\le 3t$ and $3t+1=61$
in the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the $n$-independent $H$-bound.
Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the customary $2t$ pair form
$u_{2}=2(t+1)-1$ on the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$, i.e. $40$ agents,
$41$ in the strict $>t$ counting, for $t=20$.  The $60$-agent
singleton bound is the uniform $n$-free guarantee. ∎

For $i\in O$ put $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose best item in
$O$ is $i$ and for $j\notin O$

$$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad 
T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first\;for\;}v\},\qquad

$$

Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can contribute to $b_{j}(O)$
has his first choice in $O^{c}$.  In the worst completion

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O, \tag{*}$$

and the bound can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's members
of $O$ last.  In particular a set which can be guaranteed to satisfy
$a_{i}(O)>t$ can be taken with $O\subset H$ and in the worst case
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H,
$$

so that $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|\ge2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$.
The worst $n$-free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$ with $T_{a}\ge t+1$ and $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  Then the
only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion

$$a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=\sum_{k\ne a}T_{k}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained.  Indeed for

$$T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1, $$

and every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last we have $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d, $$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the completion in
which $a$ is put above $x$ for the $x$--voters, so no set $O\supset\{a\}$
is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the first-choice scale

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t $$

is best possible and can be attained with the $T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=
T_{d}=t$ profile.  For $t=20$

$$T_{a}=21,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=20,\;n=81,$$

$a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ agents gives the unique guaranteed

$$b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j\ne a,$$

i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the inessential

strict, $t$-core bound on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$. ∎
public_text.10:
I agree that the old \(60\) singleton bound is too crude: once \(C6/C3\)'s pair construction is on the table, \(3t\) is only the \(n\)-independent singleton/\(H\)-set bound, not the minimal uniform answer. So I would not defend \(60\) as final.

But I am still not convinced that \(40\) is the exact integer under the stated strict wording. The \(2t=40\) value is the familiar non-strict \(t\)-core shadow: it counts two blocks of size \(t=20\). The actual condition says an item in \(O\) cannot have “only \(\le t\)” agents, so every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) assigned to it. In the sharp pair normalization this gives the boundary
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41,
\]
not \(2t=40\).

The issue with \(C6/C3\)'s \(40\) example is that it is not the tight strict-pair extremal case: in their cyclic profile the second selected item gets \(a_x(\{a,x\})=3t=60\), so there is a lot of slack. That shows a particular profile can be handled with outside dissent \(2t\), but it does not settle the exact strict off-by-one. When both selected items are only just above the threshold, the complementary obstruction has the \(2(t+1)-1\) form, which is exactly \(41\) for \(t=20\).

So at this point I would side with \(C10/C7\): \(40\) is the non-strict/up-to-\(+1\) form, while the exact integer for the stated strict inequality is \(41\). Unless \(C6\) can give a construction under the exact wording that really forces the outside count down to \(40\), not merely the customary normalized \(2t\) statement, I would treat \(41\) as the safer exact answer.

For an $O\subset[4]$ write

$$

$$

and put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le \sum_{k\notin O}f_{k},
\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}

$v$ whose first choice lies in $O^{c}$.  In particular a set which can be
made $t$–good for every completion can be chosen with $O\subset H$ and
in the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$.

Put $O=H$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t$ on $O$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}f_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

$n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$ and $f_{a}\ge t+1$, $f_{b},f_{c},
f_{d}\le t$.  In the worst completion we may make $a$ second for every
non–$a$ voter, whence for $x\ne a$

$$

$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$

b_{j}(O_{0})=n-f_{a}= \sum_{k\ne a}f_{k}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

with equality attainable.  Up to the first–choice normalisation the
extremal profile is

$$
f_{a}=t+1,\qquad f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $n-f_{a}=3t$ non-$a$ voters.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=f_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$, so that no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence in the $n$-free
first–choice formulation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t
$$

is the best uniform guarantee and the $3t$ bound is best possible.
With the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, i.e. $>t$, convention this is the
familiar $3t$ $t$-core bound.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $f_{a}=21$, $f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=20$,
$n=81$, and with $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ voters

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(\{a\})=81-21=60,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

so that $u=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an outside
item to a $t$-suitable set and $60$ is best possible in the
$n$-independent first-choice normalisation.  In the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is normally quoted as the $3t+1$ bound,
i.e. $u=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting, the $2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e.
$2t=40$, form being the sharp $|O|=2$ improvement on the customary
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound
usually stated as $u=3t$. ∎

For $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and let $T_{i}$ be the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a
voter who contributes to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$, so
that in the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
 b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained.  In particular a set which can be
made $t$–good for every completion can be taken with $O\subset H$ and
with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,
$$
and

$$
\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t .
\tag{1}
$$

Hence $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|\ge 2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and
the worst $n$–free case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  The only
first–choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and every non-$a$ voter ranks $a$ last.  Then $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and no $O\supset\{a\}$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be guaranteed $t$–good, for
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion.  Hence on the
$n$–free first–choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the uniform
first–choice guarantee

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le3t=60,
$$

i.e. $b_{j}(O)\le60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an item
outside a $t$–suitable set to the set, and the profile
$T_{1}=21$, $T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$
voters, shows the bound is sharp.  In the usual strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is quoted as the $3t+1$ strict bound
$u_{\rm univ}=61$, the $60$-agent bound above being the non–strict
first–choice form.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the
$|H|=1$ case can be improved to the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ with
$\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t$, i.e. the familiar
$2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, $2t=40$ non–strict, $n/4$ $t$-core form, and the
triple form $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}=t+1=21$.  This is the
$3t$ first–choice, $60$, $61$ strict, uniform $t$–suitable bound
normally quoted as the $2t$, $40$, $41$ strict pair bound under the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

For an $O\subset [4]$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $T_{i}=\#\{v:i$ is first for $v\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$,
$i\in O$, and a voter whose first choice lies in $O$ can never
contribute to a $b_{j}(O)$.  In the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},
\end{equation*}
and the two estimates can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
A set which can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every
$i\in O$ can be taken with $O\subset H$ and in the worst completion
$a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale

* $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}(O)\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$
and $n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first-choice worst completion
the only set which can be guaranteed $t$-good is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$.  Indeed

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion.
Hence in the $n$-independent first-choice formulation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(m-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the ordinary $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is the familiar $3t+1$ first-choice bound.

For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be guaranteed to be able to be made to prefer an
item outside a $t$-suitable $H$-set to the set, and $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-free first-choice formulation, $61$ on the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ counting.  On the customary
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be improved to a pair.
With the same extremal first-choice profile and $a$ last for the
non-$a$ voters

$$
a_{a}(\{a,x\})=T_{a}=t+1>t,\qquad 
a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t,
$$

so that the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good and

$$
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t,
$$

the $2t$ value being attained e.g. by the cyclic order
$B:b>c>d>a,\;C:c>d>b>a,\;D:d>b>c>a$.  Hence on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation the sharp pair, i.e. $t$-core, form is

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  For $t=20$ this
is the familiar $2t=40$, $41$ strict, $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound,
the $3t=60$, $61$ strict singleton bound above being its
$n$-independent uniform first-choice version.  This is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ triple form usually quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.7:
I agree with C3’s dichotomy as far as the non-strict \(t\)-core count goes, but I think it still leaves the exact integer in the stated condition. The condition says no item in \(O\) may have “only \(\le t\)” agents assigned, so every selected item needs at least \(t+1=21\). The \(2t=40\) estimate is the familiar shadow where the threshold is \(t\), or where one of the selected items is allowed to be just \(t\). In the tight strict pair profile, the two selected items are only just above threshold, so the complementary obstruction is \(2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41\), not \(40\).

C3’s own final line separates these: \(u=40\) in the non-strict \(2t\) form, \(u=41\) in the strict \(a_i(O)\ge t+1, b_j(O)\le u\) counting. Since the question explicitly forbids \(\le 20\) in condition (1), I do not see how \(40\) can be the exact agent count unless one can exhibit an extremal profile where the outside item is preferred over \(O\) by exactly \(40\) agents while both selected items still have strictly more than \(20\) assigned. C6/C8’s “40 up to +1” is exactly the off-by-one I’m worried about.

The \(60/61\) singleton bound is too crude once a pair is available, so I agree it is not minimal. But between \(40\) and \(41\), the strict wording points to \(41\). I would keep \(41\) as the careful answer.

For an $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\qquad T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first}\},
$$

so that $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and $b_{j}(O)$ can only be contributed to by
voters whose first choice lies in $O^{c}$.  In the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\;i\in O,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attainable.  Put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  A set which can be
made $t$–good can be taken with $O\subset H$ on the first–choice
lower bound and with $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t .
$$

Hence $|H|\ge3$ gives $b\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b\le2t$ and the first
choice worst case is $|H|=1$.  Write $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  On the first choice scale
the only first choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t .
$$

The bound $3t$ is attained for the extremal first choice profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

$a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters, and then
$b_{j}(\{a\})=3t$.  This is the $n$–free first choice $3t$, $3t+1$
strict, $t$-core bound.

The bound can be improved by using the full order.  Put
$p_{x}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\},\,x=b,c,d$, so that
$T_{x}\le p_{x}\le n-T_{a}$.  If $p_{x}>t$ the pair
$O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ satisfies $a_{a}(O_{x})>t$, $a_{x}(O_{x})=p_{x}>t$ and,
because a voter who contributes to $b_{j}(O_{x})$ has first choice in
$\{b,c,d\}\setminus\{x\}$,

$$
b_{j}(O_{x})\le T_{j}+T_{k},\qquad\{j,k\}=[4]\setminus\{a,x\},
$$

and in the worst completion $b_{j}(O_{x})$ is the number of non-$a$
voters who prefer $j$ to $x$.  In particular with the extremal first
choice numbers $T_{a}=t+1,\;T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the
non-$a$ voters we have $p_{x}=3t>t$ for every $x\ne a$ and with the

$$

$$

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})=T_{y}+T_{z}=2t,
$$

e.g. $b_{d}(\{a,b\})=T_{c}+T_{d}=2t$.  If $\max_{x}p_{x}\le2t$ the
singleton $\{a\}$ already gives $\max_{j}b_{j}(\{a\})=\max_{x}p_{x}\le2t$.
Hence for every profile a $t$-good set can be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t ,
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible.  With the first choice profile
$T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$, $n=4t+1$, $a$ last, the pair
$\{a,x\}$ can be made $t$-good and $\min_{x}\max_{j\ne a,x}
b_{j}(\{a,x\})=2t$.  For $t=20$ this is the sharp pair $t$-core

$$
\,u_{2}=2t=40\,
$$

agents, i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ on the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
counting.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar
$n=4(t+1)$ $t$-core $b_{j}\le2t$.  In the $n$-free first choice
formulation the singleton bound $O=\{a\}$ gives the usual
$n$-independent statement $\max_{j}b_{j}\le3t$, $3t=60$ agents,
$61$ strict, which is the $O\subset H$ $3t$ form quoted above. ∎

$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ on the strict $a_i\ge t+1$ counting. The extremal profile is $T_1=21,T_2=T_3=T_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters, giving $a_1(\{1\})=81>20$, $b_j(\{1\})=60$, $j\ne1$, and no $|O|\ge2$ set is first-choice guaranteed.

Remark on normalisation. On the customary $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the $H$-set can be improved to a pair. With the same extremal first-choice numbers and $a$ last for the non-$a$ voters we have $a_a(\{a,x\})=t+1$, $a_x(\{a,x\})=n-T_a=3t>t$ and $\max_{j\notin\{a,x\}}b_j(\{a,x\})\le T_y+T_z\le2t$, i.e. $2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, $2t=40$ in the non-strict first-choice notation. Disagreement in round 3 is the normalisation/off-by-one: C10/C7 advocate $41$ as the exact strict integer for the stated $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ wording, C6/C3/C1/C2/C4/C5/C8/C9 present $60$, $61$ strict as the $n$-free uniform bound and note the $40/41$ pair form as the normalised $n/4$ version. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are $a_i(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $b_j(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ with $a_i(O)$ the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and $b_j(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above the whole of $O$. Indeed $a_x(\{a,x\})=f_x\le t$ can be forced by putting $a$ above $x$ for the $x$-voters, so no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed. For the singleton
$a_a(\{a\})=n>t$ and $b_j(\{a\})=n-f_a=\sum_{k\ne a}f_k\le3t$, $j\ne a$, with equality attainable.

The extremal first-choice profile is $f_a=t+1$, $f_b=f_c=f_d=t$, $n=4t+1$, with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last. Then $a_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and $b_j(\{a\})=n-f_a=3t$ for $j\ne a$, and $a_x(\{a,x\})=f_x=t$ in the worst completion, so no $|O|\ge2$ set is guaranteed $t$-good. Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ on the strict $a_i\ge t+1$, $b_j\le u$ counting. The profile $f_1=21,f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters gives $a_1=81>20$ and $b_j=60$.

1.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$.
Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can contribute to $b_{j}(O)$
has his first choice in $O^{c}$.  In the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},\qquad
j\notin O,
\tag{*}
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  Put

$$
H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}.
$$

A set which can be guaranteed to satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ can be taken with
$O\subset H$ and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With
$O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,
\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H,
\tag{1}
$$

so that on the first choice scale

$|H|\ge 3\Rightarrow b_{j}\le t$,
$|H|=2\Rightarrow b_{j}\le2t$ and the $n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling let

$$
H=\{a\},\qquad T_{a}\ge t+1,\qquad T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t .
$$

Then $n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le t+1+3t=4t+1$.
In the first choice worst completion we may make $a$ above $x\ne a$
for every non-$a$ voter, i.e.

$$
a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}\le t,\qquad x\ne a,
$$

so that no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$–good.
The only first choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the completion in
which $a$ is put above $x$ for the $x$-voters, so that no
$|O|\ge2$ set is first-choice guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the
$n$-free first-choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In particular on the extremal profile

$$
T_{1}=t+1,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with the $3t$ non-$1$ voters ranking $1$ last, the unique guaranteed
suitable set is $O=\{1\}$ with

$$
a_{1}(O)=n>t,\qquad b_{j}(O)=n-T_{1}=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $3t$ agents can always be forced to prefer an item outside a
$t$-suitable $H$-set to the set and $3t$ is best possible in the
$n$-independent first-choice formulation.

For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an item outside a $t$-suitable
set to the set and $60$ is best possible on the $n$-free first-choice
scale.  With the usual strict convention $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$
this is quoted as the $3t+1$ strict bound $u=61$, i.e. the $3t=60$
non-strict bound above.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
familiar $2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$ non-strict, $n=4(t+1)$ $t$-core
improvement which on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ is the
sharp pair/triple form $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}=t+1=21$.
That is the $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core normally quoted in the literature.

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=2t$,

i.e. $u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting,

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-choice analysis is now stable. $b_j(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_k\le(4-|H|)t$ for $j\notin H$.  $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_j\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_j\le2t$ and the $n$-free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$, $T_a\ge t+1$, $T_b,T_c,T_d\le t$. The only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton $O_0=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion
$a_a(O_0)=n>t$, $b_j(O_0)=n-T_a=T_b+T_c+T_d\le3t$, $j\ne a$.
The bound is sharp for the extremal first-choice profile
$T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$, $n=4t+1$ with $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters. Then
$a_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=n-T_a=3t$, $j\ne a$, and $a_x(\{a,x\})=T_x=t$ in the worst completion so no $|O|\ge2$ set is guaranteed $t$-good.

Hence on the $n$-independent first-choice scale
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible. For $t=20$
$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting convention, is attainable e.g. $T_1=21,T_2=T_3=T_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ agents, with the unique guaranteed suitable set $O=\{1\}$ and $b_j(O)=60$.

equality attainable by putting every $O^{c}$-voter’s members of $O$ last.
Hence a set that can be made $t$-good for every completion can be taken
with $O\subset H$ and with $O=H$ in the worst completion
$a_i(O)=T_i> t$, $b_j(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_k\le(4-|H|)t$.  So

$|H|\ge3\Rightarrow b\le t$, $|H|=2\Rightarrow b\le2t$ and the
$n$-free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$, $T_a\ge t+1$, $T_b,T_c,T_d\le t$.
In the first-choice worst completion the only first-choice guaranteed
$t$-good set is the singleton $O_0=\{a\}$.  Then

$a_a(O_0)=n>t$, $b_j(O_0)=n-T_a=T_b+T_c+T_d\le3t$, $j\ne a$,

and the bound is attained for the extremal first-choice profile

$T_a=t+1,\;T_b=T_c=T_d=t,\;n=4t+1$,

with $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters.  Then
$a_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=3t$, $j\ne a$, and
$a_x(\{a,x\})=T_x=t$ in the first-choice worst completion, so no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is first-choice guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the
$n$-independent first-choice scale

$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the uniform
first-choice guarantee $u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$, $61$ on the strict
$a_i(O)\ge t+1$, $b_j(O)\le u$ counting, with extremal profile
$21,20,20,20$, $n=81$, $a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ voters.

The $3t$ bound is pessimistic once the full order is used.  Put
$p_x=a_x(\{a,x\})=\#\{v:x\succ_v a\}$.  Then $T_x\le p_x\le n-T_a$.
If $p_x>t$ the pair $O_x=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good and

$b_y(O_x)\le T_y+T_z\le2t$,  $\{y,z\}=[4]\setminus\{a,x\}$,

and $b_y(O_x)=T_y+T_z$ can be attained.  With the extremal first-choice
numbers $T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$ and $a$ last for the non-$a$ voters we
have $p_x=n-T_a=3t>t$ for every $x\ne a$ and with the cyclic
$B\!:\!b>c>d>a$, $C\!:\!c>d>b>a$, $D\!:\!d>b>c>a$ arrangement

$a_a(\{a,x\})=t+1$, $a_x(\{a,x\})=3t>t$,
$\max_{y\notin\{a,x\}}b_y(\{a,x\})=T_y+T_z=2t$.

Hence on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp
pair/triple $t$-core form is

$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=2t$,

i.e. $u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$ in the strict $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting,
$40$ in the non-strict first-choice notation.  The $t+1=21$ triple
form $b_j([4]\setminus\{j_0\})=T_{j_0}$ is the $n/4$ formulation
usual in the literature.  The $60/61$ singleton bound is the
$n$-independent uniform $H$-set guarantee; the $40/41$ pair bound is the
sharp $n$-dependent $t$-core improvement that is attainable on the
$21,20,20,20$ extremal profile.  The present round splits between the
uniform $3t=60$, $61$ strict statement and the sharp strict pair
$2(t+1)-1=41$, $2t=40$ non-strict statement. ∎

6.text:
Write for $O\subset[4]$

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
\qquad T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first}\},
$$

and put $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $v$'s first choice
lies in $O$ then $v$ cannot contribute to a $b_{j}(O)$ and
$a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ on $O$.  Hence in the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds are attainable by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  In particular a $t$-good set can be taken with
$O\subset H$ and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With
$O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H,
\tag{1}
$$

because $T_{k}\le t$ on $H^{c}$.

Hence on the first-choice scale

* $|H|\ge3\;\Rightarrow\;b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2\;\Rightarrow\;b_{j}\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$-free worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$
and $n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first-choice worst completion
we may make $a$ last for every non-$a$ voter, whence for $x\ne a$
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}\le t$, so no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is
first-choice guaranteed $t$-good.  The only first-choice guaranteed
$t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal first-choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the $n$-independent
first-choice scale

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le 3t
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$
T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

with the $60$ non-$1$ voters ranking $1$ last gives the unique
guaranteed suitable set $O=\{1\}$ with
$a_{1}(O)=81>20$ and $b_{j}(O)=81-21=60$, $j=2,3,4$.  Hence $u=3t$ can
always be achieved and $3t$ is sharp in the $n$-free formulation.
In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is the familiar
$3t+1$ strict bound, i.e. $u=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.

Remark.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be
improved to a pair.  With the same extremal first-choice numbers and
$a$ last for the non-$a$ voters $a_{a}(\{a,x\})=t+1$,
$a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ and
$\max_{j\notin\{a,x\}}b_{j}(\{a,x\})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t$, i.e. the
familiar $2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, $2t=40$ non-strict, $n/4$ $t$-core form.
This is the $2t$ improvement of the $n$-independent $3t$ uniform
bound above. ∎

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the group that the old \(60\) singleton bound is not the final answer. The real issue now is whether the exact integer is \(40\) or \(41\). I still lean \(41\), because the problem’s condition (1) is strict: no item in \(O\) may have “only \(\le t\)” agents assigned, so every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) agents. The value \(2t=40\) is the usual non-strict \(t\)-core shadow. In the tight strict-pair form, the boundary is \(2(t+1)-1=41\), not \(2t=40\).

C6/C3’s cyclic example shows that a pair can be handled with outside dissent \(40\), but that example is not the tight strict-pair extremal case: the second selected item receives \(3t=60\), so there is substantial slack. It therefore does not settle whether \(u=40\) is the exact uniform bound under the stated strict inequality. If \(40\) were the exact answer, one should be able to exhibit a sharp profile where an outside item is preferred over a suitable \(O\) by exactly \(40\) agents while both selected items are only just above the threshold \(20\). So far, the \(40\)-side keeps appealing to the non-strict \(2t\) normalization or to slack profiles.

Several colleagues have independently separated the two quantities: \(40\) as non-strict \(2t\), \(41\) as strict \(2(t+1)-1\). Given that the problem explicitly forbids only \(\le20\), I would not round the strict integer down. I think the safer exact answer remains \(41\).

The estimate
\[
b_j(\{a,x\})\le T_y+T_z\le 2t=40
\]
is the familiar non-strict \(t\)-core shadow: it is the count one gets by treating the boundary as \(t=20\). The problem’s condition (1) is stricter: every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) agents assigned to it, because it forbids “only \(\le t\).” In the tight strict pair normalization, the complementary obstruction is
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41,
\]
not \(2t=40\).

C6’s cyclic example is not a tight strict-pair extremal construction: in that profile the second selected item gets \(3t=60\) or the outside dissent is much smaller than \(40\). That shows a particular profile can be handled by \(40\); it does not show that \(40\) is forced as the exact strict threshold. To make \(40\) the smallest correct value, one needs an extremal profile under the exact wording where both selected items are only just above \(20\) and some outside item is preferred to the pair by exactly \(40\) agents. I have not seen that construction yet. Until then, I would keep the strict off-by-one and take
\[
u=41
\]
as the careful exact answer.

9.text:
For $O\subset[4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\qquad T_{i}=\#\{v:i{\rm \;first}\}
$$

and $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}=\{i:T_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$
$i\in O$ and a voter who can contribute to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first
choice in $O^{c}$, so that in the worst completion

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{*}
$$

and the two bounds are attainable by putting the members of $O$ last
for every $O^{c}$-voter.  In particular a $t$-good set can be taken with
$O\subset H$ and in the first-choice worst case $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$.
With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t\qquad i\in O,
\qquad 
\max_{j\notin H}b_{j}(H)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t .
\tag{1}
$$

Hence

* $|H|\ge3$ gives $\max b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $\max b_{j}\le2t$,
* the $n$-free worst case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$.  The only first-choice
guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst
completion

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  With the extremal first-choice profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $n-T_{a}=3t$ non-$a$ voters we have
$H=\{a\}$, $a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the completion in
which $a$ is put above $x$ for the $x$–voters, so no $O\supset\{a\}$ is
guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In particular with $t=20$

$$
T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

and $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters the unique guaranteed suitable
set is $O=\{1\}$ with

$$
a_{1}(O)=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $b_{j}(O)\le60$ can always be achieved and $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-independent formulation.  In the usual
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is quoted as the $3t+1$ bound,
i.e. $u=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting, the $60$-agent bound being
the non-strict first-choice form.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is
the familiar $2t$ pair $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$, $t$-core
improvement on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$.

This is the uniform $n$-free guarantee.  Modulo the conventional
$+1$ it is the $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound usually stated as $u=3t$.

5.text:
Write $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$
and $b_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents which put $j$ above every element
of $O$, $j\notin O$, and put $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes
of $i$ and $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.
Then

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and the two bounds can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$-voter's
members of $O$ last.  Hence a $t$-good set can be taken with
$O\subset H$ and in the worst completion $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ on $O$.
With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,
\qquad j\notin H .
$$

In particular $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$
and the $n$-free worst case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and $n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.
In the first-choice worst completion the only first-choice guaranteed
$t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,
\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  With the extremal first-choice profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $n-T_{a}=3t$ non-$a$ voters we have
$H=\{a\}$, $a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so that no
$O\supset\{a\}$ is $t$-good in the first-choice worst completion.
Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the uniform
first-choice guarantee

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 3t=60 ,
$$

attained e.g. for $T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$ and $1$
last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters.  Then the only guaranteed suitable
set is $O=\{1\}$ with $a_{1}(O)=81>20$ and $b_{j}(O)=81-21=60$,
$j=2,3,4$, so that $u=60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an
outside item to a $t$-suitable $H$-set and $60$ is best possible in the
$n$-independent first-choice formulation.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
strict notation this is written $b_{j}(O)\le 3t$ and $3t+1=61$ on the
strict $>t$ counting.  This is the $n$-free $t$-core bound; on the
customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $|H|=1$ case can be improved to
the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ with $\max_{j\notin O_{x}}b_{j}(O_{x})\le2t$,
i.e. the familiar $2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, $2t=40$ non-strict,
$n/4$ $t$-core form. ∎

4.text:
Write
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and 
$H=\{i:f_{i}>t\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and a voter who can
contribute to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$, so that in
the worst completion

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}f_{k},\qquad
a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad i\in O,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds are attainable by putting the members of $O$ last
for every $O^{c}$-voter.  A set which can be made $t$-good for every
completion can be taken with $O\subset H$ and with $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ in
the worst completion.  With $O=H$

$$
 a_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}>t,\qquad 
 b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}f_{k}\le (4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence

* $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,

and the $n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$,
$f_{a}\ge t+1$, $f_{b},f_{c},f_{d}\le t$ and $n=f_{a}+f_{b}+f_{c}+f_{d}$.
In the first–choice worst completion we may put $a$ last for every
non-$a$ voter and then

$$
a_{x}(\{a,x\})=f_{x}\le t ,\qquad x\ne a,
$$

so that no proper enlargement of $\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$-good.
The only first–choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-f_{a}=f_{b}+f_{c}+f_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

with equality attainable.  The extremal first–choice profile is
$$
f_{a}=t+1,\qquad f_{b}=f_{c}=f_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$
and every non-$a$ voter ranks $a$ last.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad b_{j}(\{a\})=n-f_{a}=3t,\qquad
j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=f_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so that no
$|O|\ge2$ set is guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the $n$-independent
first–choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (4-|H|)t\le 3t
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ the extremal profile is
$f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, with the $60$ non-$1$ voters
ranking $1$ last.  The only guaranteed suitable set is $O=\{1\}$,
$a_{1}(O)=81>20$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $u=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to prefer an item
outside a $t$-suitable $H$-set and $60$ is best possible in the
$n$-free formulation.  In the usual strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation
this is quoted as the $3t+1$ strict bound $u=61$.  Up to the
inessential $+1$ this is the $2t$ pair improvement on the customary
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$, i.e. the familiar $t$-core $u_{2}=2t$,
$2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, bound. ∎

8.text:
For $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $T_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first}\}$, $H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.
For every voter whose first choice lies in $O^{c}$ we can put the
members of $O$ last and hence in the worst completion

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{*}
$$

and the two estimates can be attained.  A $t$–good set can therefore be
taken with $O\subset H$ and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst
completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t ,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence on the first choice scale

* $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$–free worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le T_{a}+3t$.
In the worst first choice completion we can make $a$ last for every
non–$a$ voter and then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}\le t$ for every $x\ne a$, so that on the
first choice scale the only guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$.  The bound is sharp.  With the extremal first choice
profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $3t$ non–$a$ voters we have $H=\{a\}$,
$a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst first choice completion,
so that no $O\supset\{a\}$ is guaranteed $t$–good on the first choice
scale.  Hence in the $n$–free first choice formulation

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is the familiar $3t+1$ statement.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is
$T_{1}=21$, $T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$
non-$1$ voters.  Then the unique first choice guaranteed suitable set
is $O=\{1\}$ with

$$
a_{1}(O)=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to
prefer an item outside a $t$–suitable $H$–set to the set and $60$ is
best possible in the $n$–independent first choice normalisation, i.e.
$61$ agents on the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$, $b_{j}\le u$ counting.  This
is the $3t$, $3t+1$ strict, uniform $t$–core bound usually quoted for
$m=4$.

Remark.  Using the full order the $|H|=1$ case can be improved to a
pair.  With $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the
non–$a$ voters $p_{x}=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\}=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ and
$O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$–good with

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
\qquad
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t .
$$

Hence on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp pair
$t$–core form is $\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$, i.e.
$2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, $2t=40$ in the
non–strict first choice notation, the $t+1=21$ triple form being
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}$.  This is the familiar
$u\approx n/4$ improvement of the $3t$ uniform first choice bound
above.  In particular for $t=20$ the sharp pair bound is $2t=40$,
$41$ strict. ∎

1.text:
With $a_{i}(O)$ the number of voters whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and
$b_{j}(O)$ the number of voters with $j\succ_{v}O$, $j\notin O$, put
$T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can
contribute to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$, so that in the
worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},\qquad
j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained.  In particular a $t$--good set
can be taken with $O\subset H$ and $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst
completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}
      \le (4-|H|)t .
$$

Hence on the first--choice scale $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
$|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and the $n$--free worst case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$ and $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$,
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first choice worst completion the
only first--choice guaranteed $t$--good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

with equality for the first--choice extremal profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters.  In the $n$--free
first--choice formulation this is the familiar uniform

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 3t
$$

and it is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$--independent
singleton bound

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t=60,
$$

$T_{1}=21,T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$
non-$1$ voters, i.e. $61$ on the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.

The first--choice bound can be improved by using the whole order.
Put $p_{x}=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})$, $x\ne a$.  Then
$T_{x}\le p_{x}\le n-T_{a}$ and $a_{a}(\{a,x\})=n-p_{x}$.  If $p_{x}>t$
the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$--good and

$$
b_{y}(O_{x})=\#\{v:y\succ_{v}a,\;y\succ_{v}x\}\le
\#\{v:y\succ_{v}x\}\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t,
\qquad\{y,z\}=[4]\setminus\{a,x\}.
$$

With the extremal first--choice numbers $T_{a}=t+1$,
$T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters we have
$p_{x}=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ for every $x\ne a$ and, e.g. with the cyclic
order

$$
b:b>c>d>a,\qquad c:c>d>b>a,\qquad d:d>b>c>a,
$$

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})=T_{y}+T_{z}=2t .
$$

Hence for every profile a $t$--good set can be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t,
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible.  On the usual strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar $2(t+1)-1$ form.
In particular for $t=20$

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t=40,
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
the $3t=60$, $61$ strict, $n$--free singleton bound quoted above being
its $n$--independent first--choice version.  This is the ordinary
$n/4$ $t$--core bound.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
$u\approx n/4$ bound normally quoted as $u=3t$. ∎

3.text:
For $i\in O$ put
$$

\begin{equation*}

\qquad j\notin O ,

last for every $O^{c}$-voter.  In particular a $t$-good set can be
