completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence on the first–choice scale

* $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,

and the $n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  The only first–choice guaranteed
$t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst
completion

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained.  The extremal first–choice profile is

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so that no
$|O|\ge2$ set is first–choice guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the
$n$-free first–choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ voters gives the unique first–choice

usual strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ convention this is

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, $40$ agents in the non-strict $2t$ first-choice
notation.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar $u\approx n/4$ pair
bound $40$, $41$ strict, the $3t=60$, $61$ strict singleton bound
above being its $n$-free uniform first-choice version.  This is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ triple form usually quoted in the literature. ∎

For an $O\subset [4]$ write

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  Then

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two estimates can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$–voter's
members of $O$ last.  In particular a set which can be guaranteed to
satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can be taken with $O\subset H$
and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With $O=H$

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t,
\qquad j\notin H .
\end{equation*}
Hence on the first–choice scale

* $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$–free worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first–choice worst completion the
only first–choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

\begin{equation*}
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne a,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attained.  The extremal first–choice profile is

\begin{equation*}
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
\end{equation*}
with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

\begin{equation*}
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
\end{equation*}
and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the first–choice
worst completion, so that no $O\supset\{a\}$ is first–choice
guaranteed $t$–good.  Hence on the $n$-free first–choice scale

\[
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t,
\]

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is the familiar $3t+1$ first–choice bound.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $T_{1}=21,T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$,
$n=81$, and with the $60$ non-$1$ voters ranking $1$ last

\[
a_{1}(\{1\})=81>20,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{1\})=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

so that $b_{j}(O)\le60$ can always be achieved and $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-free first–choice formulation.  In the strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ counting this is the $3t+1=61$
statement usually quoted as the uniform $t$-suitable bound.

Remark.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be
improved by using the full order.  With the extremal first–choice
numbers $T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the non-$a$
voters $p_{x}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$, $x\ne a$, so that the pair
$O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$–good and

\[
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t .
\]

Hence on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation

\[
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
\]

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
convention, $2t=40$ in the non–strict first–choice notation,
the familiar $u\approx n/4$ $t$–core improvement of the $3t$ uniform
bound.  For $t=20$ this is the sharp pair form $40$, $41$ strict,
the $60$, $61$ strict singleton bound above being its $n$–free
uniform $H$–version. ∎

public_text.10:
I agree with the group that the old \(60\) singleton bound is not the final answer. The real issue now is whether the exact integer is \(40\) or \(41\). I still lean \(41\), because the problem’s condition (1) is strict: no item in \(O\) may have “only \(\le t\)” agents assigned, so every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) agents. The value \(2t=40\) is the usual non-strict \(t\)-core shadow. In the tight strict-pair form, the boundary is \(2(t+1)-1=41\), not \(2t=40\).

C6/C3’s cyclic example shows that a pair can be handled with outside dissent \(40\), but that example is not the tight strict-pair extremal case: the second selected item receives \(3t=60\), so there is substantial slack. It therefore does not settle whether \(u=40\) is the exact uniform bound under the stated strict inequality. If \(40\) were the exact answer, one should be able to exhibit a sharp profile where an outside item is preferred over a suitable \(O\) by exactly \(40\) agents while both selected items are only just above the threshold \(20\). So far, the \(40\)-side keeps appealing to the non-strict \(2t\) normalization or to slack profiles.

Several colleagues have independently separated the two quantities: \(40\) as non-strict \(2t\), \(41\) as strict \(2(t+1)-1\). Given that the problem explicitly forbids only \(\le20\), I would not round the strict integer down. I think the safer exact answer remains \(41\).
public_text.7:
At this point I would not defend the \(60/61\) singleton bound as final; C3/C6 are right that once a pair is available, the \(3t\) \(H\)-set estimate is not minimal. But I also do not think C6’s \(40\) settles the exact integer under the stated wording.

The estimate
\[
b_j(\{a,x\})\le T_y+T_z\le 2t=40
\]
is the familiar non-strict \(t\)-core shadow: it is the count one gets by treating the boundary as \(t=20\). The problem’s condition (1) is stricter: every selected item must have at least \(t+1=21\) agents assigned to it, because it forbids “only \(\le t\).” In the tight strict pair normalization, the complementary obstruction is
\[
2(t+1)-1=2\cdot 21-1=41,
\]
not \(2t=40\).

C6’s cyclic example is not a tight strict-pair extremal construction: in that profile the second selected item gets \(3t=60\) or the outside dissent is much smaller than \(40\). That shows a particular profile can be handled by \(40\); it does not show that \(40\) is forced as the exact strict threshold. To make \(40\) the smallest correct value, one needs an extremal profile under the exact wording where both selected items are only just above \(20\) and some outside item is preferred to the pair by exactly \(40\) agents. I have not seen that construction yet. Until then, I would keep the strict off-by-one and take
\[
u=41
\]
as the careful exact answer.

$T_{1}=21$, $T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$
non-$1$ voters.  Then the unique first choice guaranteed suitable set
is $O=\{1\}$ with

$$
a_{1}(O)=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to
prefer an item outside a $t$–suitable $H$–set to the set and $60$ is
best possible in the $n$–independent first choice normalisation, i.e.
$61$ agents on the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$, $b_{j}\le u$ counting.  This
is the $3t$, $3t+1$ strict, uniform $t$–core bound usually quoted for
$m=4$.

Remark.  Using the full order the $|H|=1$ case can be improved to a
pair.  With $T_{a}=t+1$, $T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the
non–$a$ voters $p_{x}=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\}=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ and
$O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$–good with

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
\qquad
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t .
$$

Hence on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp pair
$t$–core form is $\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t$, i.e.
$2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, $2t=40$ in the
non–strict first choice notation, the $t+1=21$ triple form being
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j_{0}\})=T_{j_{0}}$.  This is the familiar
$u\approx n/4$ improvement of the $3t$ uniform first choice bound
above.  In particular for $t=20$ the sharp pair bound is $2t=40$,
$41$ strict. ∎
public_text.1:
With $a_{i}(O)$ the number of voters whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and
$b_{j}(O)$ the number of voters with $j\succ_{v}O$, $j\notin O$, put
$T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can
contribute to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$, so that in the
worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},\qquad
j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and the two bounds can be attained.  In particular a $t$--good set
can be taken with $O\subset H$ and $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst
completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}
      \le (4-|H|)t .
$$

Hence on the first--choice scale $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
$|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$ and the $n$--free worst case is $|H|=1$.
Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$ and $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$,
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first choice worst completion the
only first--choice guaranteed $t$--good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

with equality for the first--choice extremal profile

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters.  In the $n$--free
first--choice formulation this is the familiar uniform

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 3t
$$

and it is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$--independent
singleton bound

$$
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t=60,
$$

$T_{1}=21,T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$
non-$1$ voters, i.e. $61$ on the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.

The first--choice bound can be improved by using the whole order.
Put $p_{x}=\#\{v:x\succ_{v}a\}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})$, $x\ne a$.  Then
$T_{x}\le p_{x}\le n-T_{a}$ and $a_{a}(\{a,x\})=n-p_{x}$.  If $p_{x}>t$
the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$--good and

$$
b_{y}(O_{x})=\#\{v:y\succ_{v}a,\;y\succ_{v}x\}\le
\#\{v:y\succ_{v}x\}\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t,
\qquad\{y,z\}=[4]\setminus\{a,x\}.
$$

With the extremal first--choice numbers $T_{a}=t+1$,
$T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters we have
$p_{x}=n-T_{a}=3t>t$ for every $x\ne a$ and, e.g. with the cyclic
order

$$
b:b>c>d>a,\qquad c:c>d>b>a,\qquad d:d>b>c>a,
$$

$$
a_{a}(O_{x})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(O_{x})=3t>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})=T_{y}+T_{z}=2t .
$$

Hence for every profile a $t$--good set can be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t,
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible.  On the usual strict
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar $2(t+1)-1$ form.
In particular for $t=20$

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t=40,
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting,
the $3t=60$, $61$ strict, $n$--free singleton bound quoted above being
its $n$--independent first--choice version.  This is the ordinary
$n/4$ $t$--core bound.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
$u\approx n/4$ bound normally quoted as $u=3t$. ∎

For $i\in O$ put
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and $T_{i}=\#\{v:i$ is first for $v\}$, 
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}$ and a voter who can
contribute to $b_{j}(O)$ has his first choice in $O^{c}$ and in the
worst completion

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k} ,
\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and the two estimates can be attained by putting the members of $O$
last for every $O^{c}$-voter.  In particular a $t$-good set can be
taken with $O\subset H$ and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst
completion.  With $O=H$

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le (4-|H|)t,\qquad j\notin H .
$$

Hence on the first–choice scale

* $|H|\ge3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,

and the $n$–free worst case is $|H|=1$.  Up to relabelling let
$H=\{a\}$, $T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  The only first–choice guaranteed
$t$-good set is the singleton $O_{0}=\{a\}$ and in the worst
completion

$$
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le 3t,\qquad j\ne a,
$$

and the bound is attained.  The extremal first–choice profile is

$$
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

$$
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
$$

and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ in the worst completion, so that no
$|O|\ge2$ set is first–choice guaranteed $t$-good.  Hence on the
$n$-free first–choice scale

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$
T_{1}=21,\;T_{2}=T_{3}=T_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

$a$ last for the $60$ non-$a$ voters gives the unique first–choice
suitable set $O=\{1\}$ with

$$
a_{1}(O)=81>20,\qquad b_{j}(O)=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents can always be forced to
prefer an item outside a $t$-suitable $H$-set and the $60$ is best
possible in the $n$-independent first–choice formulation.  In the
usual strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ convention this is
the $3t+1$ statement, $u=61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.

Remark.  On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be
improved to a pair.  With the extremal first–choice numbers and $a$
last for the non-$a$ voters

$$
a_{a}(\{a,x\})=t+1,\qquad a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t,
$$

so the pair $O_{x}=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good and

$$
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t,
$$

the $2t$ value being attained e.g. by the cyclic order
$B:b>c>d>a$, $C:c>d>b>a$, $D:d>b>c>a$.  Hence on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp $t$-core form is

$$
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}\ge t+1$
convention, $40$ agents in the non-strict $2t$ first-choice
notation.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar $u\approx n/4$ pair
bound $40$, $41$ strict, the $3t=60$, $61$ strict singleton bound
above being its $n$-free uniform first-choice version.  This is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ triple form usually quoted in the literature. ∎

For an $O\subset [4]$ write

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
and $T_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$H=\{i:T_{i}>t\}$.  Then

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_{i}\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k},
\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
and the two estimates can be attained by putting every $O^{c}$–voter's
members of $O$ last.  In particular a set which can be guaranteed to
satisfy $a_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can be taken with $O\subset H$
and with $a_{i}(O)=T_{i}$ in the worst completion.  With $O=H$

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)\ge T_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t,
\qquad j\notin H .
\end{equation*}
Hence on the first–choice scale

* $|H|\ge 3$ gives $b_{j}\le t$,
* $|H|=2$ gives $b_{j}\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$–free worst case.

Up to relabelling let $H=\{a\}$,
$T_{a}\ge t+1$, $T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\le t$ and
$n=T_{a}+T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}$.  In the first–choice worst completion the
only first–choice guaranteed $t$–good set is the singleton
$O_{0}=\{a\}$ and

\begin{equation*}
a_{a}(O_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{0})=n-T_{a}=T_{b}+T_{c}+T_{d}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne a,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attained.  The extremal first–choice profile is

\begin{equation*}
T_{a}=t+1,\qquad T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
\end{equation*}
with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last.  Then

\begin{equation*}
a_{a}(\{a\})=4t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{a\})=n-T_{a}=3t,\qquad j=b,c,d,
\end{equation*}
and $a_{x}(\{a,x\})=T_{x}=t$ for every $x\ne a$ in the first–choice
worst completion, so that no $O\supset\{a\}$ is first–choice
guaranteed $t$–good.  Hence on the $n$-free first–choice scale

\[
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_{k}\le(4-|H|)t\le3t,
\]

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict
convention this is the familiar $3t+1$ first–choice bound.

\[
a_{1}(\{1\})=81>20,\qquad 
b_{j}(\{1\})=81-21=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,

improved by using the full order.  With the extremal first–choice
numbers $T_{a}=t+1,T_{b}=T_{c}=T_{d}=t$ and $a$ last for the non-$a$
voters $p_{x}=a_{x}(\{a,x\})=n-T_{a}=3t>t$, $x\ne a$, so that the pair

\[
\max_{y\notin O_{x}}b_{y}(O_{x})\le T_{y}+T_{z}\le2t .
\]

\[
\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=2t,
\]

i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)-1=41$ agents in the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
convention, $2t=40$ in the non–strict first–choice notation,
the familiar $u\approx n/4$ $t$–core improvement of the $3t$ uniform
bound.  For $t=20$ this is the sharp pair form $40$, $41$ strict,
the $60$, $61$ strict singleton bound above being its $n$–free
uniform $H$–version. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-choice scale is the persistent worst-case. Put $T_i$ = # first-choice votes for $i$, $H=\{i:T_i>t\}$, $a_i(O)$ = # voters whose best in $O$ is $i$, $b_j(O)$ = # voters with $j\succ_v O$. Then $a_i(O)\ge T_i$ and any voter contributing to $b_j(O)$ has his first choice in $O^c$, so in the worst completion

$a_i(O)\ge T_i$, $ \ b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_i\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_k$,

and both bounds are attainable by putting $O^c$-voters’ members of $O$ last. A $t$-guaranteed set can be taken with $O\subset H$ and with $O=H$ we have $a_i(O)\ge T_i>t$ and $\max_{j\notin H}b_j(H)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_k\le(4-|H|)t$.

* $|H|\ge3\Rightarrow b\le t$,
* $|H|=2\Rightarrow b\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$-free worst case.

Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$, $T_a\ge t+1$, $T_b,T_c,T_d\le t$. The only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is $O_a=\{a\}$. In the worst completion $a_a(O_a)=n>t$ and

$b_j(O_a)=n-T_a=T_b+T_c+T_d\le3t$, $j\ne a,$

attainable. The extremal first-choice profile is $T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$, $n=4t+1$ with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last, i.e. $a_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=n-T_a=3t$, $j\ne a$, and $a_x(\{a,x\})=T_x=t$ in the completion which kills the pairs. Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale $\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$. Example $T_1=21,T_2=T_3=T_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters gives $a_1(\{1\})=81>20$, $b_j(\{1\})=60$, $j\ne1$, and no $|O|\ge2$ set is first-choice guaranteed. With the strict $a_i\ge t+1$ wording the statement is often quoted as $3t+1=61$.

The current round disagreement is the normalisation/off-by-one. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 present the $n$-free $3t=60$ uniform bound and note the normalised $n=4(t+1)$ improvement to a pair/triple. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue for the strict pair form $2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$ non-strict, obtained on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ where $O_x=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good with $a_a=t+1$, $a_x=3t>t$ and $\max b\le T_y+T_z\le2t$. That is the familiar $u\approx n/4$, $u_0=t+1=21$ triple form and $u=2t=40/41$ pair form. The $40$ vs $41$ split is the strict $>t$ vs non-strict $t$ counting.

I keep the problem as stated with no bound on $n$: the smallest uniform $u$ is $3t=60$, best possible, $61$ on the fully strict $>t$ counting convention, and $2t=40$, $41$ strict, is the sharp $n=4(t+1)$ normalised pair/triple improvement. Unresolved is which normalisation the problem setter intends; the text as written has no $n$ bound, hence the $n$-free $60$ is the literal uniform guarantee. ∎

The first-choice scale is the persistent worst-case. Put $T_i$ = # first-choice votes for $i$, $H=\{i:T_i>t\}$, $a_i(O)$ = # voters whose best in $O$ is $i$, $b_j(O)$ = # voters with $j\succ_v O$. Then $a_i(O)\ge T_i$ and any voter contributing to $b_j(O)$ has his first choice in $O^c$, so in the worst completion

$a_i(O)\ge T_i$, $ \ b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_i\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_k$,

and both bounds are attainable by putting $O^c$-voters’ members of $O$ last. A $t$-guaranteed set can be taken with $O\subset H$ and with $O=H$ we have $a_i(O)\ge T_i>t$ and $\max_{j\notin H}b_j(H)\le\sum_{k\notin H}T_k\le(4-|H|)t$.

* $|H|\ge3\Rightarrow b\le t$,
* $|H|=2\Rightarrow b\le2t$,
* $|H|=1$ is the $n$-free worst case.

Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$, $T_a\ge t+1$, $T_b,T_c,T_d\le t$. The only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is $O_a=\{a\}$. In the worst completion $a_a(O_a)=n>t$ and

$b_j(O_a)=n-T_a=T_b+T_c+T_d\le3t$, $j\ne a,$

attainable. The extremal first-choice profile is $T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$, $n=4t+1$ with every non-$a$ voter ranking $a$ last, i.e. $a_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=n-T_a=3t$, $j\ne a$, and $a_x(\{a,x\})=T_x=t$ in the completion which kills the pairs. Hence on the $n$-free first-choice scale $\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$. Example $T_1=21,T_2=T_3=T_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters gives $a_1(\{1\})=81>20$, $b_j(\{1\})=60$, $j\ne1$, and no $|O|\ge2$ set is first-choice guaranteed. With the strict $a_i\ge t+1$ wording the statement is often quoted as $3t+1=61$.

The current round disagreement is the normalisation/off-by-one. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 present the $n$-free $3t=60$ uniform bound and note the normalised $n=4(t+1)$ improvement to a pair/triple. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue for the strict pair form $2(t+1)-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$ non-strict, obtained on the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ where $O_x=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good with $a_a=t+1$, $a_x=3t>t$ and $\max b\le T_y+T_z\le2t$. That is the familiar $u\approx n/4$, $u_0=t+1=21$ triple form and $u=2t=40/41$ pair form. The $40$ vs $41$ split is the strict $>t$ vs non-strict $t$ counting.

I keep the problem as stated with no bound on $n$: the smallest uniform $u$ is $3t=60$, best possible, $61$ on the fully strict $>t$ counting convention, and $2t=40$, $41$ strict, is the sharp $n=4(t+1)$ normalised pair/triple improvement. Unresolved is which normalisation the problem setter intends; the text as written has no $n$ bound, hence the $n$-free $60$ is the literal uniform guarantee. ∎

On the $n$-free first-choice scale $\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.

For $t=20$ this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee $u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$, $61$ on the strict $a_i\ge t+1$, $b_j\le u$ counting. Example $f_1=21,f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the $60$ non-$1$ voters gives $a_1=81>20$ and $b_j=60$.

Remark on normalisation. On the customary normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $|H|=1$ case can be improved to a pair. With $f_a=t+1$, $f_x=t$ and $a$ last for the non-$a$ voters $a_a(\{a,x\})=t+1$, $a_x(\{a,x\})=n-f_a=3t>t$ and $\max_{j\notin\{a,x\}}b_j\le T_y+T_z\le2t$, the $2t$ value attained by the cyclic second-preference profile. Hence on $n=4(t+1)$ the sharp pair form is $\min_O\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=2t$, i.e. $u_2=2(t+1)-1=41$ strict, $2t=40$ non-strict, and the triple form gives $u_0=t+1=21$. This is the $u\approx n/4$ $t$-core bound quoted by C3,C6 and the source of the $40/41$ vs $60/61$ disagreement.

Current debate is whether the problem intends the unrestricted $n$ uniform guarantee, which is $3t=60$, or the customary $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, which is $2t=40$, $41$ strict. The public round 4 consensus remains the $n$-free singleton bound $3t=60$, $61$ strict, with the $2t=40$, $41$ strict values being the normalised pair improvement. Unresolved is the off-by-one strict convention; I keep the uniform $u=60$, $61$ strict, as the literal unrestricted answer, with the normalised $41$ noted as the usual $n/4$ $t$-core figure.

The first-choice / H-analysis is now the stable backbone of the discussion.  
Write $T_i$ for first-choice votes, $f_i(O)$ for best-in-$O$ votes and $b_j(O)$
for agents who rank $j$ above every member of $O$.  $f_i(O)\ge T_i$ and in the
worst completion $f_i(O)=T_i$ can be attained by putting all $O^{c}$ voters’
members of $O$ last.  Hence a set that can be guaranteed $t$-good for every
completion can be taken with $O\subset H=\{i:T_i>t\}$ and in the worst
completion $f_i(O)=T_i$.

With $O=H$ we have $f_i(O)\ge T_i>t$ on $O$ and
$b_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}T_i\le\sum_{k\notin O}T_k\le(4-|H|)t$ for $j\notin H$.
$|H|\ge3$ gives $b_j\le t$, $|H|=2$ gives $b_j\le2t$ and the $n$-free worst
case is $|H|=1$.

Up to relabelling $H=\{a\}$, $T_a\ge t+1$, $T_b,T_c,T_d\le t$.
The only first-choice guaranteed $t$-good set is the singleton
$O_0=\{a\}$ and in the worst completion $f_a(O_0)=n>t$,
$b_j(O_0)=n-T_a=T_b+T_c+T_d\le3t$, $j\ne a$.
The bound is sharp for the extremal first-choice profile
$T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$, $n=4t+1$ with $a$ last for the $3t$ non-$a$ voters.
Then $f_a(\{a\})=4t+1>t$, $b_j(\{a\})=3t$, $j\ne a$, and
$f_x(\{a,x\})=T_x=t$ in the worst completion so no $|O|\ge2$ set is
first-choice guaranteed $t$-good.

Hence on the $n$-independent first-choice scale
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(4-|H|)t\le3t$ and $3t$ is best possible.
For $t=20$ this is the $n$-independent singleton bound
$u_{\rm unif}^{\min}=3t=60$ agents, $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting
convention, attained e.g. $T_1=21,T_2=T_3=T_4=20$, $n=81$, $1$ last for the
$60$ non-$1$ voters, with the unique guaranteed suitable set $O=\{1\}$ and
$b_j(O)=60$.

This is the $n$-free $H$-set bound.  On the customary normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$ the $H$-set can be improved by using the whole order:
with $T_a=t+1$, $T_b=T_c=T_d=t$ and $a$ last for non-$a$ voters
$p_x=a_x(\{a,x\})=n-T_a=3t>t$, so the pair $O_x=\{a,x\}$ is $t$-good and
$\max_{j\notin O_x}b_j(O_x)\le T_y+T_z\le2t$.
The classic $t$-core form is therefore $\min_O\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=
\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. $u_0=t+1=21$ for the triple $[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$
and $u_2=2t$ for the pair, $2(t+1)-1=41$ on the strict $a_i(O)\ge t+1$
counting.  The $40/41$ pair value and the $21$ triple value are the
$n=4(t+1)$ improvements of the $60/61$ $n$-free uniform bound.

Current round disagreement persists:
C1,C2,C3,C4,C5,C8,C9 defend the $n$-free uniform $3t=60$ $(61$ strict$)$
singleton bound; C6,C10,C7 defend the normalised $2t=40$ $(41$ strict$)$
pair $u\approx n/4$ bound.  C10 stresses the strict $a_i(O)\ge t+1$
off-by-one giving $2(t+1)-1=41$ vs $2t=40$.

With the problem as stated, $n$ is unrestricted and the guarantee must
hold for all $n$.  The adversary can keep $p_x=a_x(\{a,x\})=T_x\le t$
by making $a$ dominate $x$ for every non-$x$ voter, so a pair cannot be

The $2t=40$, $41$ strict, $t+1=21$ values are the sharp $n=4(t+1)$

$40$ vs $41$ dispute.
